title: Characterization of in vitro and in vivo bioactivity of a ferulic acid-2-Hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin inclusion complex
text:
Characterization of in Vitro and in Vivo Bioactivity of a Ferulic Acid-2-Hydroxypropyl-β-Cyclodextrin Inclusion Complex

Abstract  
Ferulic acid (FA), a natural phenolic compound with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, exhibits limited bioavailability due to poor aqueous solubility. This study aimed to enhance its bioactivity by formulating a ferulic acid-2-hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (FA-HPβCD) inclusion complex. The complex was characterized using Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and X-ray diffraction (XRD). In vitro antioxidant activity was evaluated via DPPH and ABTS assays, while in vitro release profiles were assessed using simulated gastrointestinal fluids. In vivo bioactivity was investigated in a rat model of carrageenan-induced paw edema. The FA-HPβCD complex demonstrated improved solubility (8.2 ± 0.3 mg/mL vs. 0.12 ± 0.01 mg/mL for free FA) and sustained release in vitro. In vivo, the complex reduced paw edema by 65% at 6 hours post-induction, compared to 42% for free FA. These findings suggest that HPβCD complexation enhances FA’s bioactivity by improving solubility and stability, offering potential for therapeutic applications.

Keywords: Ferulic acid, 2-Hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin, inclusion complex, bioavailability, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory.

1. Introduction  
Ferulic acid (FA), a hydroxycinnamic acid derivative abundant in cereals and fruits, has gained attention for its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective properties [1]. However, its clinical application is hindered by poor aqueous solubility (0.02–0.1 mg/mL at 25°C) and rapid degradation under physiological conditions [2]. Cyclodextrins (CDs), cyclic oligosaccharides with hydrophobic cavities, are widely used to enhance the solubility and stability of hydrophobic drugs via inclusion complexation [3]. Among them, 2-hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (HPβCD) is favored for its high water solubility and low toxicity [4].  

Previous studies have demonstrated that CD complexation improves the bioavailability of curcumin [5] and quercetin [6], but limited research exists on FA-HPβCD complexes. This study hypothesizes that HPβCD inclusion enhances FA’s solubility, stability, and bioactivity. We characterized the FA-HPβCD complex using spectroscopic and thermal methods, evaluated its in vitro release and antioxidant activity, and assessed its anti-inflammatory efficacy in a rat model.

2. Materials and Methods  
2.1 Materials  
FA (purity ≥98%), HPβCD (degree of substitution 4.5), carrageenan, and analytical-grade solvents were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). Male Wistar rats (200–250 g) were obtained from the local animal facility.  

2.2 Preparation of FA-HPβCD Inclusion Complex  
The complex was prepared by co-evaporation: FA (1 mmol) and HPβCD (1 mmol) were dissolved in ethanol-water (1:1 v/v), stirred at 60°C for 4 hours, and evaporated under reduced pressure. The residue was lyophilized and stored at 4°C.  

2.3 Characterization  
- FTIR: Spectra were recorded on a PerkinElmer Spectrum Two (4000–400 cm⁻¹).  
- DSC: Thermal transitions were analyzed using a TA Instruments Q2000 (25–300°C, 10°C/min).  
- XRD: Crystallinity was assessed with a Bruker D8 Advance (Cu Kα radiation, 2θ range 5–40°).  

2.4 Solubility and Stability Studies  
Excess FA or FA-HPβCD was shaken in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.4) at 37°C for 24 hours. Samples were filtered and analyzed by UV-Vis spectroscopy (λ = 320 nm). Stability was tested in PBS (pH 1.2 and 7.4) at 37°C for 6 hours.  

2.5 In Vitro Release Studies  
The complex (10 mg) was placed in dialysis bags (MWCO 12 kDa) and immersed in simulated gastric fluid (SGF, pH 1.2) for 2 hours, followed by simulated intestinal fluid (SIF, pH 6.8) for 4 hours. Aliquots were analyzed by HPLC (C18 column, 0.1% acetic acid in acetonitrile, 1 mL/min).  

2.6 Antioxidant Activity  
DPPH and ABTS assays were performed as described [7]. Free FA and the complex (5–50 μM) were incubated with DPPH (0.1 mM) or ABTS⁺ radicals for 30 minutes. Absorbance was measured at 517 nm and 734 nm, respectively.  

2.7 In Vivo Anti-Inflammatory Activity  
Carrageenan-induced paw edema was induced in rats (n = 6/group) by subplantar injection of 1% carrageenan. Rats received oral FA (50 mg/kg), FA-HPβCD (equivalent to 50 mg/kg FA), or vehicle. Paw volume was measured at 0, 1, 3, and 6 hours using a plethysmometer.  

2.8 Statistical Analysis  
Data are expressed as mean ± SD. Statistical significance was determined by ANOVA (p < 0.05).  

3. Results and Analysis  
3.1 Characterization  
- FTIR: FA exhibited peaks at 1690 cm⁻¹ (C=O stretch) and 1630 cm⁻¹ (C=C stretch). In the complex, these peaks shifted to 1650 cm⁻¹ and 1610 cm⁻¹, indicating hydrogen bonding with HPβCD’s hydroxyl groups (Fig. 1A).  
- DSC: FA showed a melting endotherm at 172°C, absent in the complex, confirming amorphous inclusion (Fig. 1B).  
- XRD: FA displayed sharp peaks (2θ = 15.2°, 22.4°), while the complex was amorphous (Fig. 1C).  

3.2 Solubility and Stability  
The complex’s solubility (8.2 ± 0.3 mg/mL) was 68-fold higher than free FA (0.12 ± 0.01 mg/mL). In SGF, 12% of FA degraded within 2 hours, versus 3% in the complex. In SIF, degradation rates were 8% and 2%, respectively.  

3.3 In Vitro Release  
In SGF, 18% of FA was released from the complex within 2 hours, increasing to 75% in SIF by 6 hours (Fig. 2). Free FA released 95% in SGF within 1 hour, indicating poor stability.  

3.4 Antioxidant Activity  
The complex exhibited higher DPPH (IC50 = 12.5 ± 0.8 μM) and ABTS (IC50 = 8.7 ± 0.5 μM) scavenging activity than free FA (DPPH: 22.3 ± 1.2 μM; ABTS: 15.4 ± 0.9 μM) (Fig. 3).  

3.5 In Vivo Anti-Inflammatory Activity  
FA-HPβCD reduced paw edema by 65% at 6 hours, outperforming free FA (42%) and the vehicle group (p < 0.01) (Fig. 4).  

4. Discussion  
The FTIR, DSC, and XRD results confirm successful inclusion of FA into HPβCD’s hydrophobic cavity, forming an amorphous complex. The solubility enhancement aligns with previous studies on CD-based formulations [8]. Sustained release in SIF suggests the complex protects FA from gastric degradation, improving intestinal absorption.  

The superior antioxidant activity of the complex may result from increased solubility and reduced aggregation of FA molecules [9]. In vivo, the prolonged release profile likely contributed to its enhanced anti-inflammatory effect, as sustained FA levels inhibit pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNF-α and IL-6 [10].  

5. Conclusion  
The FA-HPβCD inclusion complex significantly improved FA’s solubility, stability, and bioactivity in vitro and in vivo. These findings support its potential for oral delivery in inflammatory and oxidative stress-related disorders. Future studies should optimize the complex’s formulation for clinical use.  

References  
[1] Kanski J, et al. (2002). *J Agric Food Chem*.  
[2] Zduńska K, et al. (2018). *Oxid Med Cell Longev*.  
[3] Loftsson T, Duchêne D. (2007). *Int J Pharm*.  
[4] Stella VJ, He Q. (2008). *Adv Drug Deliv Rev*.  
[5] Wang YJ, et al. (2011). *Carbohydr Polym*.  
[6] Mura P, et al. (2015). *Int J Pharm*.  
[7] Re R, et al. (1999). *Free Radic Biol Med*.  
[8] Cirri M, et al. (2017). *J Pharm Biomed Anal*.  
[9] Sotelo-Boyás ME, et al. (2010). *Food Chem*.  
[10] Sgarbossa A, et al. (2015). *PLoS One*.  

Figures  
Fig. 1: (A) FTIR spectra, (B) DSC thermograms, (C) XRD patterns of FA and FA-HPβCD.  
Fig. 2: Cumulative release profiles of FA and FA-HPβCD in SGF and SIF.  
Fig. 3: DPPH and ABTS scavenging activity of FA and FA-HPβCD.  
Fig. 4: Percentage inhibition of paw edema in carrageenan-induced rats.

title: Comparative transcriptome analysis uncovers regulatory roles of long non-coding RNAs involved in resistance to powdery mildew in melon
text:
Powdery mildew, caused by the fungal pathogen *Podosphaera xanthii*, is one of the most devastating diseases affecting melon (*Cucumis melo* L.) production worldwide, leading to substantial yield losses and compromised fruit quality. Conventional breeding strategies for disease resistance have primarily focused on protein-coding genes, overlooking the regulatory potential of non-coding RNAs, particularly long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs). LncRNAs, defined as transcripts longer than 200 nucleotides with limited protein-coding capacity, have emerged as critical regulators of gene expression in diverse biological processes, including stress responses and plant-pathogen interactions. Recent studies in model plants such as *Arabidopsis thaliana* and crop species like wheat and rice have demonstrated that lncRNAs modulate innate immunity by influencing chromatin remodeling, transcriptional regulation, and post-transcriptional mechanisms. However, the roles of lncRNAs in melon resistance to powdery mildew remain largely unexplored, creating a critical knowledge gap in understanding the molecular basis of disease resilience in this economically important crop.  
Here, we present a comparative transcriptome analysis of resistant and susceptible melon genotypes under powdery mildew infection, aiming to identify differentially expressed lncRNAs and elucidate their potential regulatory networks. By integrating RNA-sequencing data with co-expression and functional enrichment analyses, we identified candidate lncRNAs with predicted roles in immune signaling, cell wall reinforcement, and metabolic reprogramming. Our findings provide insights into the lncRNA-mediated regulatory mechanisms underlying melon defense responses, offering novel targets for breeding powdery mildew-resistant cultivars through molecular-assisted selection or genetic engineering approaches. This study expands the current understanding of non-coding RNA-based regulation in plant-pathogen interactions and underscores the importance of lncRNAs in agricultural trait improvement.

title: Edwardsiella tarda Sip1: A serum-induced zinc metalloprotease that is essential to serum resistance and host infection
text:
Results and Discussion

To investigate the role of *Edwardsiella tarda* Sip1 in serum resistance, we constructed a Δ*sip1* deletion mutant and assessed its survival in 50% normal human serum (NHS). After 60 minutes of incubation, the wild-type (WT) strain exhibited 78% ± 4.2% survival, whereas the Δ*sip1* mutant demonstrated significantly reduced survival at 12% ± 1.8% (*p* < 0.001, *n* = 6) (Fig. 1A). Complementation of Δ*sip1* with the full-length *sip1* gene restored survival to 65% ± 3.1%, confirming that Sip1 is critical for evading serum-mediated killing. Zymography revealed a single protease activity band (~85 kDa) in WT supernatants, absent in Δ*sip1* cultures, which was restored in the complemented strain (Fig. 1B). This activity was inhibited by 1,10-phenanthroline (a zinc metalloprotease inhibitor), confirming Sip1’s enzymatic class.

In a murine infection model, mice infected with WT *E. tarda* showed 80% mortality by day 5 post-infection (p.i.), with a bacterial burden of 1.2 × 10⁷ CFU/g in the spleen at day 3 p.i. In contrast, Δ*sip1*-infected mice exhibited only 20% mortality by day 7 p.i. and a 100-fold lower bacterial load (1.5 × 10⁵ CFU/g) in the spleen (*p* < 0.01, *n* = 10) (Fig. 1C). These data demonstrate that Sip1 is essential for systemic infection and tissue colonization.

The serum sensitivity of Δ*sip1* suggests Sip1 degrades complement components. Western blot analysis showed a 60% reduction in C3b deposition on Δ*sip1* compared to WT bacteria after serum exposure (*p* < 0.05, *n* = 3), indicating Sip1 disrupts complement activation. Additionally, Sip1’s metalloprotease activity likely cleaves other serum factors, such as antimicrobial peptides, enhancing survival. The reduced virulence of Δ*sip1* in mice underscores Sip1’s dual role in evading innate immunity and promoting dissemination. These findings align with studies on *Vibrio* and *Yersinia* proteases, which similarly degrade host defenses. However, Sip1’s unique induction by serum (3-fold upregulation in NHS vs. media) highlights its specialized adaptation to bloodstream survival. Future work will explore Sip1 substrates and its potential as a vaccine target or therapeutic inhibitor.

title: Restoration of organic-matter-impoverished arable soils through the application of soil conditioner prepared via short-time hydrothermal fermentation
text:
Restoration of Organic-Matter-Impoverished Arable Soils through the Application of Soil Conditioner Prepared via Short-Time Hydrothermal Fermentation

Abstract  
The degradation of arable soils due to organic matter depletion poses a critical threat to global food security and ecosystem sustainability. This study evaluates the efficacy of a novel soil conditioner derived from agricultural waste via short-time hydrothermal fermentation (STHF) in restoring organic-matter-impoverished soils. A 12-week field experiment was conducted on sandy loam soils with <1.2% organic matter content, comparing STHF-treated plots with control (untreated) and conventional organic amendment (compost) groups. Results demonstrated that STHF application significantly improved soil organic carbon (SOC) by 38.2%, water-holding capacity (WHC) by 27.5%, and aggregate stability by 41.3% compared to the control. Crop yield (maize) increased by 29.7% in STHF-treated plots, outperforming compost-treated plots by 12.1%. Microbial biomass carbon (MBC) and dehydrogenase activity rose by 65.8% and 54.3%, respectively, indicating enhanced microbial activity. These findings suggest that STHF-based soil conditioners offer a rapid, scalable, and eco-efficient solution for reversing soil degradation.

Keywords  
Soil restoration, hydrothermal fermentation, organic matter, soil health, sustainable agriculture.

1. Introduction  
Arable soils worldwide are experiencing unprecedented degradation, with an estimated 33% of global soils classified as moderately to highly degraded due to intensive farming practices, erosion, and organic matter (OM) loss [1]. Organic matter depletion reduces soil fertility, water retention, and carbon sequestration capacity, threatening agricultural productivity and climate resilience [2]. Traditional restoration methods, such as composting and crop rotation, are time-consuming and often inefficient in severely degraded soils [3]. Therefore, developing rapid, cost-effective, and scalable soil amendment technologies is urgent.

Hydrothermal fermentation (HTF), a thermochemical process conducted under moderate pressure (1–10 MPa) and temperature (150–250°C), has emerged as a promising method for converting lignocellulosic biomass into value-added products [4]. Short-time HTF (STHF, <24 hours) minimizes energy consumption while producing hydrochars and soluble organic compounds with high bioavailability [5]. Recent studies indicate that hydrochars derived from agricultural waste (e.g., rice straw, corn stover) can improve soil structure and nutrient retention [6]. However, the application of STHF-derived soil conditioners in organic-poor arable soils remains underexplored.

This study investigates the potential of a soil conditioner prepared via STHF using mixed agricultural waste (rice straw, cow manure, and food waste) to restore organic-matter-impoverished sandy loam soils. We hypothesize that STHF-derived amendments enhance soil physicochemical properties, microbial activity, and crop productivity more effectively than conventional compost.

2. Materials and Methods  
2.1. Preparation of Soil Conditioner  
Agricultural waste (rice straw:cow manure:food waste = 2:1:1, dry weight basis) was homogenized and subjected to STHF at 200°C for 6 hours in a batch reactor (1 MPa pressure). The resulting slurry was filtered to separate solid hydrochar (used as biochar) and liquid conditioner (rich in soluble organic acids and nutrients). The liquid conditioner was diluted with water (1:5 v/v) before application.

2.2. Experimental Design  
The field experiment was conducted on a 0.5-hectare site with sandy loam soil (pH 6.1, SOC 1.1%, total nitrogen 0.08%). Three treatments were applied in triplicate plots (10 m × 10 m each):  
- Control (CK): No amendment.  
- Compost (CM): Application of 10 t/ha of farmyard compost (SOC 25%, total nitrogen 1.2%).  
- STHF: Application of 5 t/ha of liquid STHF conditioner + 2 t/ha hydrochar.  

Maize (*Zea mays* L.) was cultivated as a test crop using standard agronomic practices. Soil samples were collected at 0–20 cm depth at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks post-treatment. Crop yield was measured at harvest.

2.3. Analytical Methods  
- Soil physicochemical properties: SOC by Walkley-Black method; WHC via saturation and oven-drying; aggregate stability using wet-sieving.  
- Biological properties: Microbial biomass carbon (MBC) by chloroform fumigation-extraction; dehydrogenase activity (DHA) using triphenyl tetrazolium chloride reduction.  
- Crop yield: Grain weight per plot adjusted to 15% moisture content.  

3. Results and Analysis  
3.1. Soil Physicochemical Properties  
STHF treatment significantly improved soil quality metrics (Table 1). SOC increased by 38.2% (from 1.1% to 1.52%) at 12 weeks, surpassing CM (22.7% increase). WHC rose from 18.3% to 23.3% in STHF plots, attributed to enhanced aggregate stability (mean weight diameter: 0.85 mm vs. 0.60 mm in CK). Compost showed slower SOC accumulation (1.38% at 12 weeks), likely due to slower decomposition rates.

Table 1. Soil properties under different treatments (mean ± SE).  
| Parameter         | CK       | CM        | STHF      |  
|-------------------|----------|-----------|-----------|  
| SOC (%)           | 1.1 ±0.1 | 1.35±0.08 | 1.52±0.07*|  
| WHC (%)           | 18.3±1.2 | 21.5±1.0  | 23.3±1.1* |  
| Aggregate stability (mm) | 0.45±0.05 | 0.72±0.06 | 0.85±0.04* |  
*p < 0.05 vs. CK.  

3.2. Soil Biological Activity  
STHF plots exhibited a 65.8% increase in MBC (284 mg/kg vs. 171 mg/kg in CK) and a 54.3% rise in DHA (18.6 μg TPF/g/day vs. 12.1 in CK) (Fig. 1). Compost increased MBC by 41.2% but had no significant effect on DHA, suggesting that STHF-derived soluble compounds more effectively stimulated microbial metabolism.

Fig. 1. Microbial biomass carbon (MBC) and dehydrogenase activity (DHA) at 12 weeks. Bars with different letters differ significantly (p < 0.05).  

3.3. Crop Yield  
Maize grain yield in STHF plots (5.8 t/ha) was 29.7% higher than CK (4.4 t/ha) and 12.1% greater than CM (5.2 t/ha) (Fig. 2). The yield increase correlated strongly with SOC (r = 0.82, p < 0.01) and WHC (r = 0.76, p < 0.01), indicating that STHF-induced soil improvements directly enhanced productivity.

Fig. 2. Maize grain yield under different treatments. Error bars denote SE.  

4. Discussion  
The superior performance of STHF over compost can be attributed to its dual action of supplying labile organic compounds (from the liquid conditioner) and stable carbon (from hydrochar). The liquid fraction provided readily available nutrients and organic acids that stimulated microbial growth, while hydrochar improved soil structure and water retention [7]. In contrast, compost relied on slower mineralization processes, limiting its short-term impact.

The rapid SOC accumulation in STHF plots (0.42% increase in 12 weeks) is notable, as natural SOC recovery in degraded soils typically requires decades [8]. This suggests that STHF-derived amendments could accelerate soil restoration timelines, offering a practical solution for regions facing severe land degradation.

Economically, STHF is advantageous due to its short processing time (<6 hours) and utilization of low-cost feedstocks. A cost-benefit analysis estimated that STHF application reduced amendment costs by 35% compared to compost while achieving better outcomes. However, scaling up STHF requires optimizing reactor designs and addressing potential emissions during hydrothermal processing.

5. Conclusion  
This study demonstrates that soil conditioners prepared via short-time hydrothermal fermentation effectively restore organic-matter-impoverished arable soils. STHF treatment significantly enhanced SOC, WHC, aggregate stability, microbial activity, and crop yield within 12 weeks, outperforming conventional compost. These findings support the adoption of STHF technology as a sustainable and rapid soil restoration strategy, aligning with global efforts to combat soil degradation and ensure food security. Future research should focus on long-term effects, optimal application rates, and life-cycle assessments to guide large-scale implementation.

title: HD-ZIP IV gene Roc8 regulates the size of bulliform cells and lignin content in rice
text:
Title: HD-ZIP IV Gene *Roc8* Regulates the Size of Bulliform Cells and Lignin Content in Rice

Abstract
Bulliform cells, specialized large, bubble-shaped cells located on the adaxial surface of rice leaves, play a critical role in leaf rolling and water conservation. Lignin, a complex polymer, contributes to mechanical strength and stress tolerance in plants. This study investigates the function of the homeodomain-leucine zipper (HD-ZIP) IV family gene *Roc8* in regulating bulliform cell size and lignin content in rice (*Oryza sativa*). Using CRISPR/Cas9-generated *roc8* knockout mutants and overexpression lines, we observed significant alterations in bulliform cell morphology and lignin accumulation. *roc8* mutants exhibited enlarged bulliform cells and reduced lignin content, whereas *Roc8*-overexpressing lines showed smaller bulliform cells and increased lignin deposition. Quantitative PCR and histological analyses revealed that *Roc8* modulates the expression of genes involved in cell expansion (e.g., *EXPANSIN*) and lignin biosynthesis (e.g., *CCR1* and *CAD2*). These findings suggest that *Roc8* integrates control over bulliform cell development and lignin metabolism, providing insights into mechanisms for improving rice adaptation to abiotic stress.

Keywords: Rice, HD-ZIP IV, Bulliform cells, Lignin, CRISPR/Cas9, Leaf morphology

Introduction
Rice (*Oryza sativa*) is a staple crop feeding over half the global population, but its productivity is threatened by abiotic stresses such as drought and salinity. Bulliform cells, located in the upper epidermis of grass leaves, facilitate leaf rolling to reduce water loss under dehydration (O'Toole and Cruz, 1980). Their size directly influences leaf rolling efficiency, with larger cells promoting more pronounced curling (Xiong et al., 2018). Concurrently, lignin, a phenolic polymer in cell walls, enhances mechanical strength and drought tolerance by limiting water loss (Li et al., 2017). However, excessive lignin can reduce biomass digestibility, posing challenges for biofuel production (Vanholme et al., 2010).

The HD-ZIP IV transcription factor family, characterized by a homeodomain and leucine zipper motif, regulates epidermal cell differentiation in plants (Nakamura et al., 2006). In rice, *Roc8* (Rice OCL4 Homolog 8) belongs to this family and is expressed in developing leaves (Wang et al., 2014). Preliminary data suggest *Roc8* may influence bulliform cell formation, but its role in lignin metabolism remains unexplored. This study aims to elucidate how *Roc8* coordinates bulliform cell size and lignin content, offering strategies to optimize rice resilience and biomass utility.

Materials and Methods
Plant Material and Growth Conditions
Rice (*O. sativa* ssp. *japonica* cv. Nipponbare) was used for all experiments. *roc8* knockout mutants were generated via CRISPR/Cas9 targeting exon 2 of *Roc8*. Homozygous T3 lines (roc8-1, roc8-2) and *Roc8*-overexpressing (OE) lines (OE-1, OE-2) under the *Ubi1* promoter were selected. Plants were grown in a greenhouse (28°C/25°C day/night, 14 h photoperiod) or hydroponically for lignin analysis.

Phenotypic Analysis
Leaf morphology was assessed at the tillering stage. Bulliform cell size was measured using scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Hitachi SU3500) on cross-sections of the third leaf. Lignin content was quantified via the acetyl bromide method (Morrison, 1972) and visualized using phloroglucinol-HCl staining.

Gene Expression Analysis
Total RNA was extracted from leaves using TRIzol (Invitrogen). cDNA was synthesized with SuperScript IV (Thermo Fisher). qPCR was performed using SYBR Green (Takara) with primers for *Roc8*, *EXPANSIN A8*, *CCR1*, and *CAD2* (Table S1). *Actin1* served as the reference gene.

Statistical Analysis
Data (n ≥ 3) were analyzed using ANOVA with Tukey’s HSD test (p < 0.05).

Results
Altered Bulliform Cell Size in *roc8* Mutants and OE Lines
SEM images revealed that *roc8* mutants had significantly larger bulliform cells (average area: 1,250 ± 90 µm²) compared to wild-type (WT; 850 ± 65 µm²; p < 0.01; Fig. 1A–B). Conversely, OE lines exhibited smaller cells (620 ± 50 µm²; p < 0.01). Leaf rolling indices (LRI) correlated with cell size: *roc8* leaves remained flat under drought (LRI = 0.2), while OE leaves rolled tightly (LRI = 0.8).

Reduced Lignin Content in *roc8* Mutants
Acetyl bromide assays showed *roc8* mutants had 18% lower lignin content (12.4 ± 0.8 mg/g DW) than WT (15.1 ± 1.1 mg/g DW; p < 0.05; Fig. 1C). OE lines accumulated 22% more lignin (18.3 ± 1.3 mg/g DW; p < 0.01). Phloroglucinol staining confirmed reduced lignin deposition in *roc8* vascular bundles and sclerenchyma (Fig. 1D).

Differential Gene Expression
qPCR revealed *Roc8* expression was absent in mutants and elevated in OE lines (Fig. 2A). *EXPANSIN A8*, a cell wall-loosening gene, was upregulated in *roc8* (3.2-fold; p < 0.01) and downregulated in OE (0.5-fold; p < 0.01; Fig. 2B). Lignin biosynthesis genes *CCR1* and *CAD2* were repressed in *roc8* (0.4- and 0.3-fold, respectively; p < 0.01) and induced in OE (2.8- and 3.1-fold; p < 0.01; Fig. 2C–D).

Discussion
This study demonstrates that *Roc8* is a dual regulator of bulliform cell size and lignin content in rice. The enlarged bulliform cells in *roc8* mutants align with their flat leaf phenotype under drought, suggesting *Roc8* normally restricts cell expansion to promote rolling. This mechanism resembles the role of *HDG11* in maize, where mutants exhibit larger bulliform cells and impaired leaf rolling (Zhao et al., 2020).

The inverse relationship between *Roc8* expression and lignin content suggests *Roc8* activates lignin biosynthesis genes like *CCR1* and *CAD2*. This is consistent with HD-ZIP IV proteins in *Arabidopsis* (e.g., *PDF2*), which regulate phenylpropanoid metabolism (Abe et al., 2003). Reduced lignin in *roc8* may enhance water permeability but compromise mechanical strength, highlighting a trade-off between drought adaptation and structural integrity.

Interestingly, *EXPANSIN A8* expression correlated negatively with *Roc8*, implying *Roc8* represses cell wall-loosening enzymes to limit bulliform cell growth. This contrasts with *OsHB4*, another HD-ZIP gene that promotes cell expansion in rice leaves (Dai et al., 2007), suggesting functional diversification within the family.

Conclusion
Our findings establish *Roc8* as a key regulator of bulliform cell development and lignin metabolism in rice. By modulating *EXPANSIN A8* and lignin biosynthesis genes, *Roc8* fine-tunes leaf morphology and cell wall composition, balancing water conservation and stress resilience. Future work could explore *Roc8*’s interaction with hormonal pathways (e.g., brassinosteroids) or its potential in breeding rice varieties with optimized biomass traits. These insights advance our understanding of HD-ZIP IV functions and offer genetic tools for improving crop performance under climate variability.

title: Water environment protection and sustainable development in townlet of China: A case study in Taicang
text: This study explores the strategies and challenges of water environment protection and sustainable development in small towns in China, with a case study focused on Taicang, a city renowned for its economic vitality and ecological conservation efforts. By analyzing the current state of Taicang's water environment, including water quality, pollution sources, and ecological health, this research identifies key factors influencing water sustainability, such as industrial discharge, agricultural runoff, and urbanization pressures. A mixed-methods approach is employed, integrating field surveys, water quality monitoring data, and policy analysis to evaluate the effectiveness of existing environmental regulations and management practices. The findings reveal that while Taicang has made significant progress in reducing industrial pollution and improving wastewater treatment, challenges persist in agricultural non-point source pollution control and public awareness enhancement. This paper proposes a series of targeted recommendations, including the promotion of green agricultural practices, strengthening of inter-departmental coordination, and enhancement of community engagement, to achieve a more balanced and sustainable water management system. The study provides valuable insights for policymakers and stakeholders in similar small towns, aiming to foster harmonious development between economic growth and environmental protection.

title: Lodging stress in cereal-effects and management: an overview
text:
Lodging Stress in Cereal: Effects and Management: An Overview

Abstract  
Lodging—the permanent displacement of cereal stems from their vertical position—poses a significant threat to global grain production, causing yield losses ranging from 10% to 50% depending on severity and crop stage. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the biomechanical, environmental, and agronomic factors contributing to lodging in cereals (e.g., wheat, rice, barley), evaluates its physiological impacts on crop growth, and assesses management strategies to mitigate risks. Data from field experiments and modeling studies highlight the interplay between stem strength, wind exposure, and nitrogen fertilization in lodging susceptibility. Innovative approaches, including breeding for lodging-resistant cultivars and precision agriculture technologies, are discussed as sustainable solutions. This overview underscores the need for integrated management to safeguard cereal productivity under climate variability.

Keywords  
Lodging, cereal crops, stem strength, yield loss, nitrogen management, breeding, climate resilience.

1. Introduction  
Lodging is a pervasive challenge in cereal agriculture, exacerbated by intensified farming practices and climate change. It occurs when stems buckle under their own weight or external forces (e.g., wind, rain), disrupting photosynthesis, grain filling, and harvestability. While wheat and rice are most affected, barley and oats also suffer significant losses. Yield reductions arise from physical grain damage, poor grain quality, and increased harvest costs. For instance, a 2022 study estimated that lodging costs the global wheat industry $3.5 billion annually. Historical data show lodging incidents have risen by 20% since 2000, linked to erratic weather patterns and high-input farming. Addressing lodging requires understanding its multifactorial causes, from plant morphology to field management. This review examines the mechanisms, impacts, and mitigation strategies for lodging in cereal crops.

2. Materials and Methods  
A meta-analysis was conducted using data from 120 peer-reviewed studies (2010–2023) and 15 field trials across temperate and tropical regions. Key variables included stem lodging index (SLI), measured via prostrate test (force required to bend stems at 45°), and root lodging resistance, assessed through pull-out tests. Environmental parameters (wind speed, rainfall) and agronomic practices (nitrogen rates, planting density) were correlated with lodging incidence using multivariate regression. Breeding trials evaluated 50 cereal genotypes for traits like culm wall thickness and lignin content. Modeling studies (e.g., APSIM, DSSAT) simulated lodging risks under future climate scenarios (RCP 4.5 and 8.5). Data were analyzed using R v4.2.1, with significance set at p < 0.05.

3. Results and Analysis  
3.1 Biomechanical Factors  
Stem strength, determined by culm diameter and lignin deposition, explained 68% of lodging variability. Wheat cultivars with SLI > 0.8 N/mm exhibited 90% lower lodging rates than susceptible varieties. Root anchorage, influenced by nodal root number and soil moisture, reduced root lodging by 45% in rice paddies.  

3.2 Environmental Triggers  
Wind speeds exceeding 8 m/s during grain filling increased lodging risk by 3.2-fold. In 2021, a typhoon in Jiangsu, China, caused 70% lodging in rice fields, with yield losses averaging 2.8 t/ha. Heavy rainfall (≥50 mm/day) softened soil, elevating root lodging by 25% in barley trials.  

3.3 Agronomic Practices  
Excess nitrogen (>180 kg N/ha) reduced stem lignin by 15%, doubling lodging incidence in wheat. Conversely, potassium fertilization at 90 kg K₂O/ha strengthened stems by 22%. Planting density >300 plants/m² shortened stem internodes but increased self-shading, raising lodging susceptibility by 18%.  

3.4 Breeding and Technological Interventions  
Genotypes with semi-dwarfing genes (e.g., *Rht-B1* in wheat) showed 50% lower lodging than tall varieties. Precision agriculture tools, such as UAV-based stem angle monitoring, enabled early detection of lodging-prone zones, reducing losses by 30% in Australian wheat fields.  

4. Discussion  
Lodging results from synergistic interactions between intrinsic plant traits and external stressors. While semi-dwarf cultivars mitigate risk, over-reliance on them may compromise biomass allocation to grains. Nitrogen mismanagement emerges as a critical modifiable factor; optimizing rates based on soil tests could cut lodging by 40%. Climate models predict a 15% rise in extreme weather events by 2050, necessitating resilient cultivars with balanced stem-root architecture. Precision technologies offer promise but require farmer training and cost-benefit analyses.  

Comparative studies reveal regional disparities: tropical rice systems prioritize root lodging resistance, while temperate wheat zones focus on stem strength. Integrating participatory breeding with agro-ecological zoning could tailor solutions to local conditions. Policy interventions, such as subsidies for lodging-resistant seeds, may accelerate adoption.  

5. Conclusion  
Lodging remains a formidable barrier to cereal productivity, with cascading effects on food security and farmer livelihoods. A holistic approach combining resistant genotypes, judicious nutrient management, and climate-smart practices is essential. Future research should explore gene-editing techniques (e.g., CRISPR for lignin biosynthesis) and AI-driven lodging prediction models. Collaborative efforts among breeders, agronomists, and policymakers will be pivotal in building lodging-resilient cereal systems for the 21st century.

title: CopulaNet: Learning residue co-evolution directly from multiple sequence alignment for protein structure prediction
text:
The accurate prediction of protein structures from amino acid sequences remains a fundamental challenge in computational biology, with profound implications for understanding protein function, disease mechanisms, and drug discovery. Traditional methods, such as homology modeling and physics-based simulations, have made significant strides but are often limited by the availability of homologous templates or the computational cost of simulating atomic interactions. The advent of deep learning has revolutionized the field, particularly with the introduction of end-to-end models that learn directly from raw sequence data. However, most existing deep learning approaches focus on capturing local or hierarchical patterns within individual sequences, overlooking the rich evolutionary information embedded in multiple sequence alignments (MSAs).

MSAs provide a window into the co-evolutionary relationships between residues, which are critical for understanding protein folding and function. Co-evolutionary signals, such as correlated mutations, can reveal spatially proximal residues in the 3D structure, even in the absence of known homologs. Despite their potential, effectively capturing and interpreting these signals remains challenging due to the high dimensionality and noise inherent in MSAs. Existing methods often rely on handcrafted features or statistical models to extract co-evolutionary patterns, which may not fully capture the complex dependencies between residues.

In this work, we introduce CopulaNet, a novel deep learning framework designed to directly learn residue co-evolution from MSAs for protein structure prediction. Our approach leverages copula functions, a probabilistic tool for modeling multivariate dependencies, to disentangle and capture the intricate co-evolutionary relationships between residues. By integrating copulas with a deep neural network architecture, CopulaNet can automatically learn hierarchical representations of co-evolutionary signals, enabling more accurate predictions of residue contacts and protein structures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CopulaNet on benchmark datasets, showing significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods and highlighting its potential to advance the field of protein structure prediction.

title: Effects of fertilization and reclamation time on soil bacterial communities in coal mining subsidence areas
text:
Results and Discussion  

Soil bacterial community diversity and composition responded significantly to fertilization and reclamation time. After 1 year of reclamation, Shannon diversity indices were 3.2 ± 0.1 in unfertilized plots and 3.8 ± 0.2 in fertilized plots (p < 0.05), indicating that fertilization enhanced microbial diversity. By year 3, diversity increased to 3.5 ± 0.1 in unfertilized plots and 4.1 ± 0.2 in fertilized plots, suggesting a cumulative benefit of prolonged nutrient input. Reclamation time alone also influenced diversity; year 3 plots exhibited 15% higher diversity than year 1 (p < 0.01), likely due to progressive soil stabilization.  

Beta diversity analysis (Bray-Curtis dissimilarity) revealed distinct clustering by treatment (PERMANOVA, R² = 0.28, p = 0.001). Fertilized plots had higher relative abundances of *Proteobacteria* (28% vs. 22%) and *Actinobacteria* (18% vs. 14%), taxa associated with organic matter decomposition and nutrient cycling. Conversely, unfertilized plots showed greater dominance of *Acidobacteria* (25% vs. 19%), which thrive in oligotrophic conditions. Reclamation time shifted community structure: year 3 plots had 12% higher *Firmicutes* abundance, linked to improved soil aggregation and carbon sequestration.  

These findings underscore synergistic effects of fertilization and time on microbial recovery. Fertilization accelerated nutrient availability, while extended reclamation allowed for ecosystem maturation. However, the dominance of copiotrophic taxa in fertilized plots raises concerns about long-term stability, warranting studies on balanced nutrient management. Our results align with prior studies in post-mining landscapes, emphasizing microbial communities as sensitive indicators of ecological restoration success.

title: Chinese Herbal Medicine Dingji Fumai Decoction for Ventricular Premature Contraction: A Real-World Trial
text:
Chinese Herbal Medicine Dingji Fumai Decoction for Ventricular Premature Contraction: A Real-World Trial

Abstract
Ventricular premature contractions (VPCs) are a prevalent form of cardiac arrhythmia associated with increased morbidity and reduced quality of life. While conventional antiarrhythmic drugs are commonly prescribed, their efficacy is often limited by side effects and variable patient responses. This real-world trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of Dingji Fumai Decoction (DFD), a traditional Chinese herbal formula, in managing symptomatic VPCs. A total of 240 patients with frequent VPCs (≥500 beats/24h) were enrolled and divided into two groups: 120 received DFD alongside standard care (DFD group), while 120 received standard care alone (control group). Over a 12-week observation period, the DFD group demonstrated a 62.5% reduction in VPC burden (p < 0.001) and significant improvements in quality of life scores (p = 0.002), compared to a 28.3% reduction in the control group. No severe adverse events were reported in the DFD group, suggesting a favorable safety profile. These findings highlight DFD as a promising complementary therapy for VPC management, warranting further exploration in larger clinical trials.

Keywords: Ventricular premature contractions, Chinese herbal medicine, Dingji Fumai Decoction, real-world trial, arrhythmia.

1. Introduction
Ventricular premature contractions (VPCs) are ectopic cardiac impulses originating from the ventricles, manifesting as irregular heartbeats or palpitations. While isolated VPCs are often benign, frequent episodes are linked to structural heart disease, heart failure, and increased mortality risk [1]. Conventional treatments, including beta-blockers and class III antiarrhythmic drugs, reduce VPC frequency but are limited by side effects such as bradycardia, fatigue, and proarrhythmia [2]. Moreover, up to 40% of patients exhibit incomplete symptom relief or drug intolerance [3], underscoring the need for alternative therapies.

Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) has long been used to manage cardiac arrhythmias, with herbal formulas targeting "heart qi deficiency" and "blood stasis"—pathological states believed to underlie VPCs [4]. Dingji Fumai Decoction (DFD), a modified classical formula, combines *Codonopsis pilosula* (Dangshen), *Ophiopogon japonicus* (Maidong), *Schisandra chinensis* (Wuweizi), and *Salvia miltiorrhiza* (Danshen) to tonify heart qi, nourish yin, and activate blood circulation [5]. Preclinical studies suggest DFD modulates ion channels and reduces oxidative stress in cardiomyocytes [6], but clinical evidence remains sparse. This real-world trial assessed DFD’s efficacy and safety in reducing VPC burden and improving patient-reported outcomes in a diverse cohort.

2. Materials and Methods
2.1 Study Design and Participants
This multicenter, open-label, real-world trial enrolled 240 adults (aged 18–75) with symptomatic VPCs (≥500 beats/24h on Holter monitoring) from three TCM hospitals in China between January 2022 and December 2023. Exclusion criteria included severe heart failure (NYHA Class IV), acute coronary syndrome, or contraindications to TCM. Patients were allocated 1:1 to the DFD or control group using stratified randomization based on age and comorbidities.

2.2 Interventions
The DFD group received a daily oral dose of 200 mL decoction (prepared from 10 g *Codonopsis*, 15 g *Ophiopogon*, 10 g *Schisandra*, and 12 g *Salvia*) alongside standard care (beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers as needed). The control group received standard care alone. Both groups were followed for 12 weeks, with assessments at baseline, 4, 8, and 12 weeks.

2.3 Outcome Measures
The primary endpoint was the percentage reduction in VPC burden (24h Holter). Secondary endpoints included quality of life (QoL) scores (Chinese version of the SF-36), symptom severity (palpitations, dizziness, chest tightness), and safety (adverse events [AEs]).

2.4 Statistical Analysis
Data were analyzed using SPSS 26.0. Continuous variables were compared via t-tests or ANOVA; categorical variables via chi-square tests. Intention-to-treat analysis was applied. A p-value <0.05 was considered significant.

3. Results and Analysis
3.1 Baseline Characteristics
Groups were comparable in age (DFD: 58.3 ± 9.2 years; control: 57.6 ± 8.7 years), sex (DFD: 52% male; control: 55% male), and comorbidities (hypertension: 45% vs. 48%; diabetes: 22% vs. 20%). Baseline VPC burden averaged 1,240 ± 320 beats/24h in both groups.

3.2 Primary Endpoint: VPC Burden Reduction
At 12 weeks, the DFD group showed a 62.5% reduction in VPC burden (from 1,250 ± 310 to 470 ± 180 beats/24h; p < 0.001), versus 28.3% in the control group (from 1,230 ± 330 to 880 ± 250 beats/24h; p = 0.02) (Figure 1). Subgroup analysis revealed greater efficacy in patients with heart failure (68% vs. 32% reduction; p = 0.01).

3.3 Secondary Endpoints: QoL and Symptoms
The DFD group reported significant improvements in SF-36 physical (Δ12.4 vs. Δ5.2; p = 0.002) and mental health scores (Δ10.8 vs. Δ4.1; p = 0.005) compared to controls. Symptom severity scores for palpitations (Δ3.2 vs. Δ1.5; p < 0.001) and chest tightness (Δ2.8 vs. Δ1.1; p = 0.001) also favored DFD.

3.4 Safety
No severe AEs occurred in either group. The DFD group reported mild gastrointestinal discomfort (8.3%) and dry mouth (5.0%), resolving spontaneously. Control group AEs included fatigue (12.5%) and bradycardia (6.7%), consistent with known drug profiles.

4. Discussion
This trial demonstrates DFD’s superiority over standard care in reducing VPC burden and improving QoL, with a safety profile comparable to placebo. The 62.5% reduction in VPCs aligns with preclinical data showing DFD’s modulation of calcium and potassium channels [6], potentially stabilizing cardiomyocyte membrane potentials. The formula’s multi-target approach—tonifying qi, nourishing yin, and activating blood—may address underlying TCM pathologies, explaining its broader symptom relief compared to single-agent conventional therapies.

Notably, DFD’s efficacy persisted across subgroups, including patients with heart failure, a population often resistant to antiarrhythmic drugs. This suggests DFD’s potential as an adjunct in complex cases, though larger trials are needed to confirm these findings. The absence of severe AEs contrasts favorably with amiodarone’s 15% discontinuation rate due to toxicity [7], positioning DFD as a low-risk alternative for drug-intolerant patients.

Limitations include the open-label design and lack of placebo control, which may introduce bias. However, real-world settings enhance generalizability, reflecting routine clinical practice. Future double-blind RCTs should explore DFD’s mechanisms and long-term outcomes.

5. Conclusion
DFD significantly reduces VPC burden and improves QoL with minimal side effects, offering a viable complementary therapy for symptomatic VPCs. Its integration into cardiology guidelines could benefit patients unresponsive to conventional treatments, pending larger-scale validation.

title: In Silico Prediction of Blood-Brain Barrier Permeability of Compounds by Machine Learning and Resampling Methods
text:
In Silico Prediction of Blood-Brain Barrier Permeability of Compounds by Machine Learning and Resampling Methods

Abstract
The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is a critical physiological structure that regulates the entry of compounds into the central nervous system (CNS). Predicting BBB permeability is essential for drug development targeting neurological disorders. Traditional experimental methods for assessing BBB permeability are time-consuming and costly, necessitating the development of in silico models. This study aimed to develop and validate machine learning (ML) models for predicting BBB permeability using a dataset of 1,200 compounds with experimentally determined logBB values. We employed various ML algorithms, including Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Gradient Boosting (GB), and applied resampling techniques such as Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) and Adaptive Synthetic Sampling (ADASYN) to address class imbalance. The models were evaluated using metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC). The GB model with ADASYN resampling achieved the highest performance, with an accuracy of 92.3%, precision of 91.5%, recall of 93.1%, F1-score of 92.3%, and AUC-ROC of 0.97. These results demonstrate the potential of ML models combined with resampling methods for accurate in silico prediction of BBB permeability, offering a valuable tool for early-stage drug discovery.

Keywords: Blood-brain barrier, machine learning, resampling methods, drug discovery, in silico prediction, logBB.

1. Introduction
The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is a highly selective semipermeable border of endothelial cells that prevents solutes in the circulating blood from non-selectively crossing into the extracellular fluid of the central nervous system (CNS). This barrier is crucial for maintaining CNS homeostasis but also poses a significant challenge for the delivery of therapeutic agents to the brain. Predicting the ability of a compound to cross the BBB is, therefore, a critical step in the development of drugs targeting neurological disorders such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and brain tumors.

Traditional methods for assessing BBB permeability involve in vitro models, ex vivo studies, and in vivo animal experiments. While these methods provide valuable insights, they are often time-consuming, expensive, and ethically concerning. In silico methods, particularly those based on machine learning (ML), offer a promising alternative by enabling high-throughput screening of compounds and predicting their BBB permeability based on molecular descriptors and structural features.

However, the development of accurate ML models for BBB permeability prediction is hindered by class imbalance, where the number of compounds that do not cross the BBB significantly outweighs those that do. Class imbalance can lead to biased models that favor the majority class, resulting in poor performance on the minority class. Resampling techniques such as Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) and Adaptive Synthetic Sampling (ADASYN) have been shown to mitigate class imbalance by generating synthetic samples for the minority class, thereby improving model performance.

This study aimed to develop and validate ML models for predicting BBB permeability using a dataset of 1,200 compounds with experimentally determined logBB values. We employed various ML algorithms, including Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Gradient Boosting (GB), and applied resampling techniques to address class imbalance. The models were evaluated using multiple metrics to ensure robust performance assessment.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Dataset
A dataset of 1,200 compounds with experimentally determined logBB values was compiled from publicly available sources, including the ChEMBL database and literature reports. The logBB value is a widely used metric for quantifying BBB permeability, where a positive logBB indicates higher permeability. Compounds were classified as BBB-permeable (logBB ≥ 0) or BBB-impermeable (logBB < 0), resulting in 450 permeable and 750 impermeable compounds.

2.2 Molecular Descriptors
Molecular descriptors were calculated using the RDKit library in Python. A total of 208 descriptors were computed, including physicochemical properties (e.g., molecular weight, logP), topological descriptors (e.g., Wiener index, Balaban index), and electrostatic descriptors (e.g., total polar surface area). Descriptors with low variance (< 0.1) or high correlation (> 0.95) were removed to reduce dimensionality and improve model performance.

2.3 Resampling Techniques
To address class imbalance, two resampling techniques were applied:
- SMOTE: Synthetic samples for the minority class were generated by interpolating between existing minority class samples.
- ADASYN: An adaptive version of SMOTE that generates synthetic samples based on the density distribution of the minority class, giving more weight to samples in less dense regions.

2.4 Machine Learning Algorithms
Three ML algorithms were employed:
- Random Forest (RF): An ensemble method that constructs multiple decision trees and aggregates their predictions.
- Support Vector Machine (SVM): A supervised learning model that identifies the hyperplane that best separates the classes.
- Gradient Boosting (GB): An ensemble method that builds trees sequentially, with each tree correcting the errors of the previous one.

2.5 Model Training and Evaluation
The dataset was split into training (70%) and testing (30%) sets. Models were trained on the training set and evaluated on the testing set using the following metrics:
- Accuracy: The proportion of correct predictions.
- Precision: The proportion of true positives among predicted positives.
- Recall: The proportion of true positives among actual positives.
- F1-score: The harmonic mean of precision and recall.
- Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC-ROC): A measure of the model's ability to distinguish between classes.

3. Results

3.1 Baseline Model Performance
Without resampling, the baseline models exhibited varying performance (Table 1). The GB model achieved the highest accuracy (85.7%), precision (84.2%), recall (87.1%), F1-score (85.6%), and AUC-ROC (0.92). However, all models showed lower recall for the minority class (BBB-permeable compounds), indicating a bias toward the majority class.

Table 1: Baseline Model Performance

| Model | Accuracy (%) | Precision (%) | Recall (%) | F1-Score (%) | AUC-ROC |
|-------|-------------|--------------|-----------|--------------|---------|
| RF    | 82.1        | 80.5         | 83.7      | 82.0         | 0.89    |
| SVM   | 83.5        | 81.9         | 85.2      | 83.5         | 0.90    |
| GB    | 85.7        | 84.2         | 87.1      | 85.6         | 0.92    |

3.2 Resampling Model Performance
After applying SMOTE and ADASYN, model performance improved significantly (Table 2). The GB model with ADASYN resampling achieved the highest accuracy (92.3%), precision (91.5%), recall (93.1%), F1-score (92.3%), and AUC-ROC (0.97). Both resampling techniques improved recall for the minority class, with ADASYN showing slightly better performance than SMOTE.

Table 2: Resampling Model Performance

| Model       | Resampling | Accuracy (%) | Precision (%) | Recall (%) | F1-Score (%) | AUC-ROC |
|-------------|------------|-------------|--------------|-----------|--------------|---------|
| RF          | SMOTE      | 88.5        | 87.9         | 89.2      | 88.5         | 0.94    |
| RF          | ADASYN     | 89.2        | 88.6         | 89.8      | 89.2         | 0.95    |
| SVM         | SMOTE      | 89.7        | 89.1         | 90.3      | 89.7         | 0.95    |
| SVM         | ADASYN     | 90.5        | 89.9         | 91.1      | 90.5         | 0.96    |
| GB          | SMOTE      | 91.2        | 90.5         | 91.8      | 91.2         | 0.96    |
| GB          | ADASYN     | 92.3        | 91.5         | 93.1      | 92.3         | 0.97    |

4. Discussion
The results demonstrate that ML models combined with resampling techniques can effectively predict BBB permeability. The baseline models, while showing reasonable performance, were biased toward the majority class, resulting in lower recall for BBB-permeable compounds. This bias is a common issue in imbalanced datasets and can lead to poor generalization on unseen data.

Resampling techniques such as SMOTE and ADASYN mitigated class imbalance by generating synthetic samples for the minority class, thereby improving model performance. ADASYN outperformed SMOTE in this study, likely due to its adaptive approach that focuses on samples in less dense regions, leading to a more balanced distribution of synthetic samples.

Among the ML algorithms tested, GB achieved the highest performance, both with and without resampling. GB's ability to build trees sequentially and correct errors iteratively makes it well-suited for imbalanced datasets. The combination of GB and ADASYN resulted in the best model, with an accuracy of 92.3% and an AUC-ROC of 0.97, indicating excellent discriminatory power.

These findings align with previous studies that have shown the effectiveness of ML models and resampling techniques for predicting BBB permeability. However, this study contributes by providing a comprehensive comparison of multiple ML algorithms and resampling methods, offering insights into the best combination for this task.

5. Conclusion
This study developed and validated ML models for predicting BBB permeability using a dataset of 1,200 compounds. The GB model with ADASYN resampling achieved the highest performance, demonstrating the potential of ML models combined with resampling techniques for accurate in silico prediction of BBB permeability. These models offer a valuable tool for early-stage drug discovery, enabling high-throughput screening of compounds and reducing the need for expensive and time-consuming experimental methods. Future work could explore the integration of additional features, such as 3D structural information, and the application of deep learning approaches to further improve model performance.

title: Dermal bioaccessibility and absorption of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in indoor dust and its implication in risk assessment
text:
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), a class of persistent organic pollutants ubiquitous in indoor dust, pose significant health risks due to their carcinogenic and mutagenic properties. Assessing dermal bioaccessibility and absorption of PAHs from dust is critical for refining human exposure models and improving risk characterization. This study systematically evaluated the dermal bioaccessibility of 16 priority PAHs in indoor dust samples collected from residential and office environments using *in vitro* physicochemically based extraction methods, including simulated sweat and sequential solvent extractions. Factors influencing bioaccessibility, such as dust particle size, organic matter content, and PAH molecular weight, were investigated. Results demonstrated that low-molecular-weight PAHs (e.g., naphthalene, phenanthrene) exhibited significantly higher dermal bioaccessibility (15–40%) compared to high-molecular-weight counterparts (e.g., benzo[a]pyrene, <5%), likely due to differences in hydrophobicity and skin penetration efficiency. Organic matter in dust was identified as a key determinant, enhancing PAH solubility and bioavailability. *In vitro* permeation studies using reconstructed human epidermis (RHE) models further revealed that only a fraction (1–10%) of bioaccessible PAHs penetrated the stratum corneum, with absorption rates varying by compound lipophilicity. These findings underscore the importance of integrating dermal bioaccessibility data into probabilistic risk assessments to avoid overestimation or underestimation of exposure. Current regulatory frameworks, which primarily rely on total PAH concentrations, may inadequately capture real-world dermal risks. By incorporating *in vitro* bioaccessibility and absorption metrics, this study provides a refined approach for evaluating PAH-related health risks in indoor settings, supporting the development of targeted mitigation strategies and public health guidelines.

Key features:  
- Focuses on *in vitro* methods and mechanistic insights.  
- Highlights molecular weight and organic matter as key factors.  
- Emphasizes risk assessment implications and regulatory gaps.

title: Antibiotic misuse among university students in developed and less developed regions of China: a cross-sectional survey
text:
Antibiotic Misuse Among University Students in Developed and Less Developed Regions of China: A Cross-Sectional Survey

Abstract  
This study investigates antibiotic misuse behaviors among university students in developed and less developed regions of China through a cross-sectional survey. A total of 1,200 participants (600 from developed regions and 600 from less developed regions) completed a structured questionnaire assessing antibiotic knowledge, self-medication practices, and sources of antibiotics. Results revealed that 42% of students in developed regions and 58% in less developed regions reported self-medicating with antibiotics without a prescription in the past year. Common reasons included mild illnesses (e.g., colds) and perceived time efficiency. Misconceptions about antibiotic efficacy against viral infections were prevalent, with 35% of students in developed regions and 52% in less developed regions believing antibiotics cure colds. Logistic regression identified lower educational attainment, limited access to healthcare, and peer influence as significant predictors of misuse in less developed regions, while convenience and prior positive experiences drove misuse in developed regions. These findings underscore the need for region-specific interventions to promote prudent antibiotic use.

Keywords: Antibiotic misuse, university students, developed regions, less developed regions, China, self-medication.

1. Introduction  
Antibiotic resistance (ABR) is a global public health crisis exacerbated by inappropriate antibiotic use, including self-medication and non-prescription access [1]. In China, antibiotics are widely available over-the-counter in many regions, contributing to misuse, particularly among populations with limited healthcare access or awareness [2]. University students, a demographic transitioning to independent healthcare decision-making, are vulnerable to misinformation about antibiotics [3]. While studies have explored antibiotic misuse in China’s general population [4], regional disparities—particularly between developed and less developed areas—remain underexamined. Developed regions typically benefit from stronger healthcare infrastructure and public health campaigns, whereas less developed regions face challenges like limited medical resources and pharmaceutical regulation [5]. This study aims to compare antibiotic misuse behaviors among university students in these two settings to inform targeted interventions.

2. Materials and Methods  
A cross-sectional survey was conducted between March and June 2023 across six universities in China: three in developed regions (Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou) and three in less developed regions (Yunnan, Guizhou, Gansu). Participants were recruited via stratified random sampling to ensure representation across academic disciplines and years of study. The final sample comprised 1,200 students (600 per region), with a mean age of 21.3 years (SD = 1.8).  
Data were collected using a validated questionnaire covering: (1) demographic information (age, gender, region, academic year), (2) antibiotic knowledge (e.g., “Do antibiotics kill viruses?”), (3) self-medication practices (frequency, reasons, sources), and (4) healthcare access (e.g., proximity to clinics, insurance coverage). Responses were scored for knowledge accuracy (e.g., 1 point for correct answers to 5 knowledge questions).  
Statistical analyses included chi-square tests for categorical variables and logistic regression to identify predictors of misuse. A p-value <0.05 was considered significant.

3. Results and Analysis  
3.1 Demographics and Knowledge  
Students in developed regions scored higher on antibiotic knowledge (mean = 3.8/5) than those in less developed regions (mean = 2.9/5; p < 0.001). However, 35% of the former and 52% of the latter incorrectly believed antibiotics cure viral infections like colds.  
3.2 Self-Medication Practices  
Self-medication without a prescription was reported by 42% of students in developed regions and 58% in less developed regions (p < 0.001). Common reasons included mild symptoms (e.g., sore throat: 68% vs. 75%) and time constraints (45% vs. 32%). Antibiotics were primarily sourced from pharmacies (70% vs. 85%) or leftover supplies (20% vs. 10%).  
3.3 Predictors of Misuse  
Logistic regression revealed that in less developed regions, students with lower knowledge scores (OR = 2.1, 95% CI: 1.5–3.0) and those living off-campus (OR = 1.8, 95% CI: 1.2–2.7) were more likely to misuse antibiotics. In developed regions, convenience (OR = 1.6, 95% CI: 1.1–2.3) and peer recommendations (OR = 1.4, 95% CI: 1.0–2.0) were significant drivers.

4. Discussion  
Our findings highlight stark regional differences in antibiotic misuse among Chinese university students, driven by disparities in knowledge, healthcare access, and cultural norms. Students in less developed regions exhibited higher misuse rates, likely due to weaker regulatory enforcement and reliance on pharmacies for medical advice—a trend observed in other low-resource settings [6]. Conversely, misuse in developed regions stemmed from convenience and social influences, aligning with studies showing that overconfidence in self-diagnosis fuels irrational use [7].  
The knowledge gap between regions underscores the need for tailored education campaigns. In less developed areas, interventions should focus on pharmacists and community health workers to curb non-prescription sales, while developed regions could leverage digital platforms to counter misinformation. Policymakers must also address systemic barriers, such as uneven healthcare distribution and insurance coverage, which perpetuate inequities in safe antibiotic access.  
Limitations include self-reported data, which may underestimate misuse, and the exclusion of private universities, potentially limiting generalizability. Future research should explore longitudinal impacts of educational programs and the role of social media in shaping antibiotic attitudes.

5. Conclusion  
Antibiotic misuse among Chinese university students is influenced by regional socioeconomic factors, with less developed regions facing higher risks due to systemic vulnerabilities. Effective mitigation requires multi-faceted strategies: strengthening pharmaceutical regulations, improving healthcare accessibility, and implementing culturally appropriate education initiatives. Addressing these disparities is critical to curbing ABR and safeguarding public health in an increasingly interconnected world.

References  
[1] World Health Organization. (2020). Antibiotic resistance.  
[2] Zhang, Q. et al. (2019). *Journal of Global Health*, 9(1), 010412.  
[3] Li, Y. et al. (2021). *Antimicrobial Resistance & Infection Control*, 10(1), 15.  
[4] Wang, X. et al. (2020). *BMC Public Health*, 20(1), 1234.  
[5] National Bureau of Statistics of China. (2022). China Statistical Yearbook.  
[6] Morgan, D.J. et al. (2017). *The Lancet Infectious Diseases*, 17(3), e90–e95.  
[7] Reynolds, L. et al. (2019). *BMJ Open*, 9(5), e026481.

title: Phosphorylated kraft lignin with improved thermal stability
text:
The quest for sustainable and eco-friendly materials has intensified in recent years, driven by escalating environmental concerns and the depletion of fossil resources. Lignin, as one of the most abundant biopolymers on Earth, has garnered significant attention for its potential to serve as a renewable alternative to petroleum-based polymers. Among various types of lignin, kraft lignin stands out due to its high availability as a byproduct of the kraft pulping process, which is widely used in the paper industry. However, the direct application of kraft lignin in high-performance materials is often hindered by its inherent limitations, including low thermal stability, poor solubility, and a lack of reactive functional groups. These drawbacks necessitate chemical modifications to enhance its properties and expand its range of applications.

Phosphorylation has emerged as a promising modification technique to improve the thermal stability and functional versatility of lignin. By introducing phosphate groups, phosphorylation can enhance the intermolecular interactions within lignin, thereby improving its thermal resistance and mechanical properties. Moreover, phosphorylated lignin exhibits increased reactivity, making it suitable for further functionalization and blending with other polymers. Despite these potential advantages, research on phosphorylated kraft lignin remains relatively limited, particularly concerning its thermal behavior and the underlying mechanisms of stabilization.

This study aims to investigate the effects of phosphorylation on the thermal stability of kraft lignin, providing insights into the structural changes induced by this modification and their impact on thermal degradation pathways. By systematically analyzing the thermal properties of phosphorylated kraft lignin using advanced characterization techniques, we seek to establish a foundation for the development of high-performance lignin-based materials. The findings of this research could significantly contribute to the sustainable utilization of lignin, offering a viable route to eco-friendly materials with enhanced thermal stability for various industrial applications.

title: An alternative parameter to characterize biogas materials: Available carbon-nitrogen ratio
text:
Results and Discussion  
The available carbon-nitrogen ratio (aC/N), calculated as the fraction of labile carbon (C_avail) to total nitrogen (N_total), was evaluated across four feedstocks: corn stover (CS), food waste (FW), dairy manure (DM), and co-digested CS+FW (1:1 w/w). Labile C_avail was determined via 7-day anaerobic incubation, measuring CO₂-C release as a proxy for biodegradable carbon. CS exhibited the highest initial total C/N of 45:1 but a low aC/N of 12:1 due to only 26% of total carbon being labile (Table 1). Conversely, FW had a lower total C/N (20:1) but a higher aC/N (18:1), reflecting its 90% labile carbon fraction. DM showed minimal labile carbon (8%), resulting in an aC/N of 3:1, despite a moderate total C/N of 25:1. The co-digestion of CS+FW yielded an intermediate aC/N of 15:1, balancing labile carbon availability and nitrogen content.  

Biogas production correlated strongly with aC/N (R² = 0.92), outperforming total C/N (R² = 0.68). For instance, FW produced 420 mL CH₄/g VS despite its lower total C/N, while DM yielded only 180 mL CH₄/g VS. Ammonia inhibition in DM (NH₄⁺-N = 2,800 mg/L) aligned with its low aC/N, whereas FW’s optimal aC/N maintained NH₄⁺-N below inhibitory levels (800 mg/L). These results suggest aC/N better captures substrate dynamics by emphasizing labile carbon availability, which drives microbial activity and nitrogen utilization efficiency. Future work should validate aC/N across diverse feedstocks and operational conditions to refine its predictive accuracy for biogas optimization.
