title: A nurse-driven enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) nursing program for geriatric patients following lung surgery
text:
Title: A Nurse-Driven Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) Nursing Program for Geriatric Patients Following Lung Surgery

Abstract

Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols have demonstrated significant benefits in improving postoperative outcomes across various surgical specialties. However, their application in geriatric patients undergoing lung surgery remains underexplored. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of a nurse-driven ERAS program tailored for geriatric patients following lung surgery. A quasi-experimental design was employed, comparing outcomes between patients receiving standard care (control group, n=50) and those enrolled in the ERAS program (intervention group, n=50). The ERAS program incorporated preoperative education, optimized pain management, early mobilization, and nutritional support. Primary outcomes included length of hospital stay (LOS), postoperative complications, and readmission rates. Secondary outcomes included patient satisfaction and functional recovery. The intervention group exhibited a significantly shorter median LOS (5 days vs. 7 days, p<0.01), lower complication rates (18% vs. 36%, p=0.04), and reduced 30-day readmission rates (8% vs. 20%, p=0.03). Patient satisfaction scores were higher in the ERAS group (8.5/10 vs. 6.2/10, p<0.001). Functional recovery, measured by 6-minute walk distance at discharge, was also superior in the intervention group (320m vs. 280m, p=0.02). These findings suggest that a nurse-driven ERAS program can significantly improve postoperative outcomes in geriatric patients undergoing lung surgery, emphasizing the role of specialized nursing interventions in enhancing recovery.

Keywords: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS), Geriatric Patients, Lung Surgery, Nursing Program, Postoperative Outcomes

Introduction

Geriatric patients undergoing lung surgery face unique challenges due to age-related physiological changes, comorbidities, and reduced functional reserve, which collectively increase the risk of postoperative complications, prolonged hospital stays, and readmissions. Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols have emerged as a multidisciplinary approach to optimize perioperative care, aiming to accelerate recovery, reduce complications, and shorten hospital stays. While ERAS programs have been successfully implemented in various surgical settings, their application in geriatric populations, particularly following lung surgery, remains limited.

Nurses play a pivotal role in ERAS programs, acting as coordinators and educators to ensure adherence to protocol components. This study introduces a nurse-driven ERAS program specifically designed for geriatric patients undergoing lung surgery, focusing on preoperative education, optimized pain management, early mobilization, and nutritional support. The objective was to evaluate the impact of this program on postoperative outcomes, including length of hospital stay, complication rates, readmission rates, patient satisfaction, and functional recovery.

Materials and Methods

A quasi-experimental design was conducted at a tertiary care hospital between January 2022 and December 2023. Geriatric patients (≥65 years) scheduled for elective lung surgery were recruited and allocated to either the control group (standard care, n=50) or the intervention group (ERAS program, n=50). Exclusion criteria included emergency surgeries, severe cognitive impairment, and inability to provide informed consent.

The ERAS program consisted of:
1. Preoperative Education: Nurses provided detailed information on the surgical procedure, expected postoperative course, and ERAS components, emphasizing the importance of early mobilization and nutrition.
2. Optimized Pain Management: A multimodal analgesia regimen was implemented, combining paracetamol, NSAIDs, and opioids as needed, with regular pain assessments using a numeric rating scale.
3. Early Mobilization: Patients were encouraged to sit out of bed on the day of surgery and commence walking within 24 hours postoperatively, with daily goals set by the nursing team.
4. Nutritional Support: Oral nutritional supplements were offered if oral intake was insufficient, and enteral nutrition was initiated if necessary.

Primary outcomes included length of hospital stay, postoperative complications (e.g., pneumonia, atelectasis, deep vein thrombosis), and 30-day readmission rates. Secondary outcomes were patient satisfaction (measured using a 10-point Likert scale) and functional recovery (assessed by 6-minute walk distance at discharge). Data were analyzed using SPSS version 26, with chi-square tests for categorical variables and Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Results

Baseline characteristics were similar between groups (Table 1). The ERAS group had a significantly shorter median LOS (5 days vs. 7 days, p<0.01) and lower rates of postoperative complications (18% vs. 36%, p=0.04). The 30-day readmission rate was also lower in the ERAS group (8% vs. 20%, p=0.03). Patient satisfaction scores were higher in the ERAS group (8.5/10 vs. 6.2/10, p<0.001), and functional recovery, as measured by 6-minute walk distance, was superior (320m vs. 280m, p=0.02).

Discussion

This study demonstrates that a nurse-driven ERAS program can significantly improve postoperative outcomes in geriatric patients undergoing lung surgery. The shorter LOS in the ERAS group may be attributed to enhanced recovery processes facilitated by early mobilization and optimized pain management, reducing the risk of complications and accelerating functional recovery. The lower complication and readmission rates further underscore the program's effectiveness in mitigating risks associated with geriatric surgery.

Patient satisfaction was notably higher in the ERAS group, likely due to the proactive involvement of nurses in education and care coordination, fostering a sense of empowerment and engagement in their recovery. The improvement in functional recovery, as evidenced by increased 6-minute walk distances, highlights the importance of early mobilization and nutritional support in preserving physical function in this vulnerable population.

Conclusion

A nurse-driven ERAS program tailored for geriatric patients following lung surgery can significantly enhance postoperative outcomes, including reducing hospital stay, complication rates, and readmissions, while improving patient satisfaction and functional recovery. These findings advocate for the widespread adoption of ERAS protocols in geriatric surgical care, with nurses playing a central role in their implementation and success. Future research should focus on long-term outcomes and cost-effectiveness to further validate the benefits of such programs.

title: Ochratoxin A: Toxicity, oxidative stress and metabolism
text:
Here is a concise and SCI-style abstract for your paper:

---

Ochratoxin A (OTA), a mycotoxin produced by Aspergillus and Penicillium species, poses significant threats to human and animal health due to its widespread contamination in food and feed. This review comprehensively examines OTA's toxicity, oxidative stress mechanisms, and metabolic pathways. OTA exhibits nephrotoxic, hepatotoxic, immunotoxic, and carcinogenic properties, primarily through induction of oxidative stress, DNA damage, and apoptosis. Its pro-oxidant effects involve disruption of cellular redox homeostasis via excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and depletion of antioxidant defenses. Metabolically, OTA undergoes hydrolysis, conjugation, and hydroxylation, with cytochrome P450 enzymes playing pivotal roles in its bioactivation to reactive intermediates. The interplay between oxidative stress and metabolic activation contributes to OTA's persistent toxicity and tissue accumulation. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for developing effective detoxification strategies and risk assessment models. Future research should focus on elucidating species-specific metabolic differences and identifying biomarkers for early OTA exposure detection.  

---

This abstract maintains a formal academic tone while concisely covering key aspects of OTA research, with appropriate technical terminology and logical flow suitable for SCI journals.

title: Morphophysiological mechanism of rice yield increase in response to optimized nitrogen management
text:
Morphophysiological Mechanism of Rice Yield Increase in Response to Optimized Nitrogen Management

Abstract  
Optimized nitrogen (N) management is critical for enhancing rice yield while minimizing environmental impacts. This study investigated the morphophysiological mechanisms underlying yield improvements in rice (*Oryza sativa* L.) under optimized N regimes compared to conventional practices. Field experiments were conducted over two growing seasons, evaluating three N application strategies: conventional split N (CK), optimized N with real-time adjustment based on leaf color charts (LCC-N), and controlled-release urea (CRU-N). Results showed that optimized N management increased grain yield by 12.3–15.7% compared to CK, primarily through improved panicle density (+18.2%) and spikelet fertility (+9.5%). Physiological analyses revealed enhanced photosynthetic efficiency (Pn increased by 14.8–22.1%), prolonged leaf functional duration, and optimized N partitioning to reproductive organs. Root morphological traits, including root length density (+26.4%) and root oxidation activity (+19.3%), were significantly improved under optimized N, facilitating nutrient uptake. These findings highlight the synergistic effects of optimized N timing, form, and rate on rice morphophysiology, providing a scientific basis for sustainable N management practices.

Keywords  
Rice yield, nitrogen management, photosynthesis, root morphology, nitrogen partitioning, sustainable agriculture.

1. Introduction  
Nitrogen (N) is a key nutrient influencing rice growth and yield, but excessive or inefficient N use leads to low N use efficiency (NUE) and environmental pollution. Traditional N management often relies on fixed-rate split applications, which fail to account for dynamic crop demand and soil N supply. Optimized N strategies, such as real-time adjustments using leaf color charts (LCC) or controlled-release fertilizers (CRU), have shown promise in improving yield and NUE. However, the morphophysiological mechanisms driving these improvements remain poorly understood. This study aimed to elucidate how optimized N management enhances rice yield by examining its effects on plant morphology, photosynthetic traits, root development, and N partitioning.

2. Materials and Methods  
The experiment was conducted in a paddy field (2020–2021) using the rice cultivar *Nangyou 46*. Three N treatments were applied: (1) CK: conventional split N (180 kg N/ha, 40% basal, 30% tillering, 30% panicle initiation); (2) LCC-N: adjusted N rates (120–150 kg N/ha) based on LCC readings (threshold = 4); (3) CRU-N: single basal application of CRU (150 kg N/ha). Each treatment had three replicates in randomized complete blocks.

Plant height, tiller number, and leaf area index (LAI) were measured at key growth stages. Photosynthetic rate (Pn), stomatal conductance (gs), and chlorophyll content (SPAD) were recorded using a portable photosynthesis system. Root samples were collected at flowering to analyze root length density (RLD) and root oxidation activity (ROA). At maturity, dry matter accumulation (DMA) and N partitioning in stems, leaves, and grains were determined. Yield components, including panicle number, spikelets per panicle, and 1000-grain weight, were recorded.

3. Results and Analysis  
3.1 Yield and Yield Components  
Optimized N treatments significantly increased grain yield (Table 1). LCC-N and CRU-N achieved 12.3% and 15.7% higher yields than CK, respectively. The yield gains were attributed to a 18.2% increase in panicle density (LCC-N) and a 9.5% improvement in spikelet fertility (CRU-N). No significant differences in 1000-grain weight were observed.

Table 1. Yield and yield components under different N treatments  
| Treatment | Yield (t/ha) | Panicle Number (m²) | Spikelet Fertility (%) | 1000-Grain Weight (g) |
|-----------|--------------|---------------------|------------------------|-----------------------|
| CK        | 6.82 ± 0.34  | 285 ± 12            | 82.5 ± 3.1             | 25.6 ± 0.4            |
| LCC-N     | 7.66 ± 0.41* | 337 ± 15*           | 85.2 ± 2.8*            | 25.9 ± 0.5            |
| CRU-N     | 7.89 ± 0.38* | 321 ± 14*           | 90.3 ± 3.5*            | 26.1 ± 0.3            |
*Significant at p < 0.05 vs. CK.

3.2 Photosynthetic Traits  
Optimized N improved photosynthetic efficiency during critical stages (Fig. 1). At heading, LCC-N and CRU-N increased Pn by 14.8% and 22.1%, respectively, compared to CK. SPAD values were 8–12% higher in optimized N treatments, indicating sustained chlorophyll synthesis. The prolonged leaf functional duration under LCC-N and CRU-N contributed to a 15.3% increase in post-anthesis DMA.

3.3 Root Morphology and Activity  
Root development was significantly enhanced under optimized N (Fig. 2). CRU-N increased RLD by 26.4% in the 0–20 cm soil layer, while LCC-N improved ROA by 19.3% at flowering. These traits facilitated greater nutrient uptake, as evidenced by a 14.7% higher N accumulation in grains under CRU-N.

3.4 Nitrogen Partitioning  
Optimized N shifted N allocation toward reproductive organs (Fig. 3). At maturity, CRU-N increased grain N content by 12.8% while reducing stem N by 9.6%, compared to CK. This optimized partitioning supported spikelet development and grain filling.

4. Discussion  
The yield increases under optimized N were driven by synergistic improvements in morphophysiological traits. Higher panicle density in LCC-N resulted from balanced vegetative growth, avoiding excessive tillering under CK. Enhanced spikelet fertility in CRU-N was linked to improved N supply during meiosis, reducing spikelet degeneration.

Photosynthetic enhancements under optimized N were attributed to better N nutrition, which sustained chloroplast function and delayed leaf senescence. The higher ROA and RLD under CRU-N reflected improved root proliferation, enabling efficient N uptake despite lower total N rates. This aligns with previous studies showing that CRU reduces N loss and prolongs availability.

Optimized N partitioning to grains was critical for yield formation. The reduced stem N under CRU-N suggested improved remobilization efficiency, a key trait for high-yielding rice. These findings underscore the importance of synchronizing N supply with crop demand to maximize NUE.

5. Conclusion  
Optimized N management enhanced rice yield by improving panicle density, spikelet fertility, and photosynthetic efficiency while optimizing root development and N partitioning. CRU-N demonstrated superior performance due to its sustained N release, reducing application frequency and environmental risks. These results advocate for adopting site-specific N strategies based on real-time monitoring and controlled-release technologies to achieve sustainable rice production. Future research should explore long-term impacts on soil health and interactions with other agronomic practices.

title: Responses of paddy soil bacterial community assembly to different long-term fertilizations in southeast China
text: Paddy soils, as one of the most critical agricultural ecosystems globally, play a pivotal role in ensuring food security, particularly in regions with dense populations such as Southeast China. However, the sustainability of paddy soil productivity is increasingly challenged by intensive agricultural practices, especially long-term fertilization regimes that significantly alter soil properties and microbial communities. Bacterial communities, as essential components of soil ecosystems, are intricately involved in nutrient cycling, organic matter decomposition, and plant growth promotion, thereby directly influencing soil fertility and crop yield. Previous studies have demonstrated that different fertilization strategies, including chemical fertilizers, organic amendments, and their combinations, can differentially shape soil bacterial community composition and diversity. Nevertheless, the underlying mechanisms driving bacterial community assembly in response to long-term fertilization remain poorly understood, particularly in subtropical paddy soils characterized by high temperature and humidity. This knowledge gap hinders the development of effective soil management practices aimed at optimizing microbial functions for sustainable agriculture. Therefore, this study aims to elucidate the responses of paddy soil bacterial community assembly to various long-term fertilization treatments in Southeast China, providing insights into microbial ecology and guiding sustainable fertilization practices.

title: Effect and Molecular Mechanisms of Traditional Chinese Medicine on Tumor Targeting Tumor-Associated Macrophages
text:
Results and Discussion

Results
In this study, we evaluated the tumor-targeting efficacy of a modified traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) formulation, *Astragalus-Curcuma* (AC), in a murine colorectal cancer model. Fluorescent imaging revealed a 2.3-fold (p < 0.01) increase in AC accumulation within tumor tissues compared to non-targeted controls at 24 hours post-administration, confirming enhanced tumor targeting. Flow cytometry analysis demonstrated a significant reduction in tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) expressing the M2 marker CD206 (from 65% ± 4% to 38% ± 3%, p < 0.001) after 14 days of AC treatment, alongside a 1.8-fold increase in M1-like TAMs (CD86+; p < 0.01). Tumor growth inhibition was observed, with a 52% reduction in tumor volume (p < 0.001) and a 37% decrease in metastatic nodules (p < 0.01) in AC-treated mice versus controls.

Discussion
The enhanced tumor targeting of AC aligns with prior studies on TCM bioavailability, likely due to nano-encapsulation improving delivery to the tumor microenvironment (TME). The shift from pro-tumor M2 to anti-tumor M1 TAMs suggests AC modulates macrophage polarization via NF-κB and STAT3 pathways, as supported by *in vitro* data showing downregulated IL-10 and upregulated TNF-α secretion in AC-treated macrophages. The 52% tumor growth inhibition exceeds monotherapy benchmarks (e.g., anti-PD-1 antibodies achieve ~30–40% in similar models), indicating synergistic effects of TAM reprogramming and direct cytotoxicity. Notably, AC’s 37% reduction in metastases highlights its potential to disrupt TAM-mediated epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), a key metastatic driver. However, liver enzyme elevations (ALT/AST) in 20% of treated mice suggest dose-dependent toxicity, warranting optimization. Future studies will explore AC’s interaction with immune checkpoint inhibitors and validate biomarkers for patient stratification. These findings position AC as a promising TAM-targeted therapy, bridging TCM’s holistic principles with modern oncology.

title: Microbial carbon source utilization in rice rhizosphere soil with different tillage practice in a double cropping rice field
text:
Microbial Carbon Source Utilization in Rice Rhizosphere Soil with Different Tillage Practice in a Double Cropping Rice Field

Abstract
This study investigates the impact of different tillage practices on microbial carbon source utilization in the rhizosphere soil of a double cropping rice field. Three tillage methods were evaluated: conventional tillage (CT), no-tillage (NT), and reduced tillage (RT). Soil samples were collected during two rice growing seasons to analyze microbial community functional diversity using Biolog EcoPlates. The results indicated that NT and RT practices significantly enhanced microbial carbon source utilization efficiency compared to CT, particularly for carbohydrates and carboxylic acids. These findings suggest that conservation tillage practices can promote beneficial microbial activities in rice paddies, potentially contributing to improved soil health and agricultural sustainability.

Keywords: Tillage practices, microbial carbon utilization, rice rhizosphere, double cropping, soil health.

1. Introduction
Rice is a staple food crop for more than half of the world's population, with double cropping systems being widely adopted to enhance annual productivity. However, intensive tillage practices associated with conventional rice farming can lead to soil degradation, reduced biodiversity, and increased greenhouse gas emissions. The rhizosphere, a narrow region of soil influenced by root exudates, plays a crucial role in nutrient cycling and plant-microbe interactions. Microbial communities in the rhizosphere are responsible for decomposing organic matter and making nutrients available to plants, thus influencing crop growth and yield.

Tillage practices can significantly alter soil structure, moisture, and temperature, thereby affecting microbial community composition and function. Conventional tillage (CT), involving inversion and mixing of soil layers, often disrupts soil aggregates and microbial habitats, leading to reduced microbial diversity and activity. In contrast, conservation tillage practices such as no-tillage (NT) and reduced tillage (RT) aim to minimize soil disturbance, preserving soil structure and organic matter. These practices have been shown to enhance soil microbial biomass and activity in various cropping systems, but their effects on microbial carbon source utilization in double cropping rice fields remain poorly understood.

This study aims to compare the effects of CT, NT, and RT on microbial carbon source utilization in the rhizosphere soil of a double cropping rice field. We hypothesize that conservation tillage practices will enhance microbial functional diversity and carbon utilization efficiency, contributing to improved soil health and ecosystem functioning.

2. Materials and Methods
The study was conducted in a double cropping rice field located in [location], over two consecutive growing seasons. The experimental design consisted of three tillage treatments: CT, NT, and RT, each replicated four times in a randomized complete block design. CT involved moldboard plowing to a depth of 20 cm, followed by harrowing. NT maintained the previous crop residues on the soil surface without any soil disturbance, while RT involved minimal soil disturbance using a rotary tiller to a depth of 10 cm.

Soil samples were collected from the rhizosphere at the tillering and flowering stages of both rice crops. Microbial community functional diversity was assessed using Biolog EcoPlates, which contain 31 different carbon sources representing various chemical classes. The plates were incubated at 25°C for 7 days, and absorbance readings were taken at 590 nm every 24 hours to monitor carbon source utilization.

Average well color development (AWCD) was calculated as an indicator of overall microbial activity. Functional diversity indices, including Shannon's diversity index (H'), evenness (E), and richness (S), were derived from the absorbance data to assess microbial community structure and function.

3. Results and Analysis
AWCD values indicated that microbial carbon source utilization was significantly higher under NT and RT compared to CT at both sampling stages (P < 0.05). NT exhibited the highest AWCD values, followed by RT and CT, suggesting greater microbial activity in conservation tillage systems.

Carbon source utilization patterns varied among tillage treatments. NT and RT showed higher utilization rates for carbohydrates and carboxylic acids, which are key components of root exudates and organic matter. In contrast, CT had higher utilization rates for amino acids and polymers, possibly due to increased mineralization of organic nitrogen sources under disturbed soil conditions.

Functional diversity indices further supported these findings. NT and RT had significantly higher H' and E values compared to CT, indicating greater microbial diversity and evenness in carbon source utilization. Richness (S) was also higher under NT and RT, suggesting a broader range of carbon sources being utilized by the microbial community.

4. Discussion
The results of this study demonstrate that conservation tillage practices, particularly NT, can enhance microbial carbon source utilization in the rhizosphere soil of double cropping rice fields. The increased utilization of carbohydrates and carboxylic acids under NT and RT aligns with the hypothesis that these practices promote the growth of microbial groups specialized in degrading plant-derived organic compounds. This enhanced microbial activity can contribute to improved nutrient cycling and soil fertility, benefiting rice growth and yield.

The higher functional diversity indices observed under NT and RT suggest that these practices support a more diverse and resilient microbial community. Diverse microbial communities are better equipped to adapt to environmental changes and resist pathogen attacks, thereby enhancing ecosystem stability and productivity.

In contrast, CT's reliance on intensive soil disturbance may disrupt microbial habitats and reduce the availability of organic substrates, leading to lower microbial activity and diversity. The increased utilization of amino acids and polymers under CT could reflect a compensatory mechanism where microbes resort to alternative carbon sources due to the depletion of readily available substrates.

5. Conclusion
This study provides evidence that conservation tillage practices, particularly no-tillage, can significantly enhance microbial carbon source utilization in the rhizosphere soil of double cropping rice fields. By promoting the utilization of plant-derived organic compounds and supporting a diverse microbial community, NT and RT contribute to improved soil health and agricultural sustainability. These findings underscore the importance of adopting conservation tillage practices in rice farming systems to mitigate the negative impacts of intensive tillage and promote environmentally friendly agricultural production. Future research should focus on long-term monitoring of soil microbial communities under different tillage regimes to better understand their role in nutrient cycling and crop productivity.

title: Dominance of Fossil Fuels in Japan's National Energy Mix and Implications for Environmental Sustainability
text:
Dominance of Fossil Fuels in Japan's National Energy Mix and Implications for Environmental Sustainability

Abstract
Japan’s energy policy faces a critical tension between energy security and environmental sustainability. Despite global shifts toward renewable energy, fossil fuels remain dominant in Japan’s energy mix, accounting for 78% of total primary energy supply (TPES) in 2022. This study examines the structural drivers of fossil fuel reliance, including post-Fukushima nuclear shutdowns and industrial demand, and evaluates its environmental implications using carbon intensity metrics and emissions projections. Analysis reveals that Japan’s carbon intensity (0.36 kgCO₂/kWh in 2022) is 45% higher than the G7 average, with fossil fuels contributing 92% of electricity-sector emissions. While renewable energy adoption has grown by 12% annually since 2013, it remains constrained by grid instability and policy fragmentation. The paper concludes that Japan’s current trajectory risks non-compliance with its 2030 emissions targets under the Paris Agreement, urging accelerated renewable integration and nuclear restarts to balance energy security with sustainability.

Keywords: Fossil fuels, energy transition, carbon emissions, renewable energy, Japan, energy policy.

 Introduction
Japan’s energy landscape is shaped by its resource scarcity, industrial intensity, and historical reliance on imported fuels. Following the 2011 Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster, the country shut down 54 nuclear reactors, eliminating 30% of its pre-crisis electricity generation capacity. This void was filled by fossil fuels, particularly liquefied natural gas (LNG) and coal, which now constitute 78% of Japan’s TPES (Agency for Natural Resources and Energy [ANRE], 2023). While Japan has pledged to reduce emissions by 46% below 2013 levels by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2050, its fossil fuel dominance raises questions about the feasibility of these goals. This study analyzes the structural and policy drivers of Japan’s energy mix, quantifies its environmental impacts, and assesses pathways to decarbonization.

 Materials and Methods
Data Sources: Primary data were sourced from ANRE’s 2023 Energy White Paper, the International Energy Agency (IEA), and Japan’s Ministry of the Environment (MOE). Secondary data included peer-reviewed studies on Japan’s energy transition and IPCC emissions scenarios.

Analytical Framework:
1. Energy Mix Analysis: Quantified the share of fossil fuels, nuclear, and renewables in TPES and electricity generation (2010–2022).
2. Carbon Intensity Calculation: Derived CO₂ emissions per unit of energy generated (kgCO₂/kWh) using IPCC emission factors.
3. Emissions Projections: Modeled 2030 emissions under three scenarios: (1) business-as-usual (BAU), (2) accelerated renewables, and (3) nuclear restarts + renewables.
4. Policy Review: Evaluated the Sixth Strategic Energy Plan (2021) and Green Growth Strategy (2020) for alignment with decarbonization targets.

 Results
1. Current Energy Mix:
- Fossil fuels dominate TPES (78%), with LNG (32%), oil (29%), and coal (17%) as primary sources (Figure 1).
- Renewables account for 8% of TPES (hydro 3%, solar 2.5%, biomass 1.5%, wind 1%), while nuclear contributes 6% (post-restarts).
- Electricity generation: Fossil fuels supply 72% (coal 32%, LNG 40%), renewables 18%, and nuclear 10% (2022 data).

2. Carbon Intensity:
- Japan’s electricity carbon intensity (0.36 kgCO₂/kWh) exceeds the G7 average (0.25 kgCO₂/kWh) by 45% (Figure 2).
- Coal accounts for 65% of electricity-sector emissions, followed by LNG (27%) and oil (8%).

3. Emissions Projections:
- BAU Scenario: Emissions reach 1,120 MtCO₂ by 2030 (12% above 2013 levels), missing the 46% reduction target.
- Accelerated Renewables: Solar capacity triples to 150 GW by 2030, reducing emissions to 980 MtCO₂ (3% above 2013).
- Nuclear + Renewables: Restarting 20 reactors (20 GW) alongside renewables cuts emissions to 850 MtCO₂ (15% below 2013).

 Discussion
1. Drivers of Fossil Fuel Reliance:
- Energy Security: Japan imports 92% of its energy, with LNG contracts diversified across 20 countries to mitigate supply risks.
- Industrial Demand: Heavy industries (steel, cement) rely on coal for cost-effective baseload power, resisting decarbonization pressures.
- Policy Inertia: The feed-in tariff (FIT) program for renewables faces grid integration challenges, while nuclear restarts are delayed by regulatory hurdles and public opposition.

2. Environmental Implications:
- Emissions Trajectory: Under BAU, Japan’s 2030 emissions will exceed its Paris Agreement pledge by 220 MtCO₂, risking global climate goals.
- Air Quality: Fossil fuel combustion contributes to PM2.5 levels exceeding WHO guidelines in urban areas (e.g., Tokyo, Osaka).
- Ecosystem Risks: Coastal coal plants threaten marine biodiversity, while LNG terminals disrupt fisheries.

3. Barriers to Transition:
- Grid Instability: Solar and wind’s intermittency requires costly battery storage, which remains underdeveloped (installed capacity: 2 GW in 2022).
- Financial Constraints: Renewable investments lag due to high upfront costs and low profitability compared to fossil fuels.
- Social Resistance: Communities near nuclear sites oppose restarts, while coal workers demand job security amid plant closures.

4. Global Context:
Japan’s fossil fuel subsidies ($16 billion in 2022) contradict G7 commitments to phase out inefficient fossil fuel support. Its LNG demand also sustains global fossil infrastructure, undermining green transitions elsewhere.

 Conclusion
Japan’s fossil fuel dominance reflects a trade-off between energy security and sustainability, exacerbated by post-Fukushima policy shifts and industrial inertia. While renewables have grown, their contribution remains insufficient to meet 2030 targets without nuclear restarts or stricter coal phaseout policies. To align with the Paris Agreement, Japan must:
1. Accelerate renewable deployment through grid modernization and financial incentives.
2. Restart nuclear reactors with enhanced safety measures to displace coal.
3. Implement carbon pricing to internalize fossil fuel externalities.
4. Strengthen international cooperation to reduce LNG dependency and fund green technologies.

Failure to act risks irreversible climate impacts and economic costs from stranded fossil assets. Japan’s transition offers lessons for resource-poor nations balancing energy security with decarbonization, underscoring the need for integrated, equity-focused policies.

title: Responses of Morphology, Gas Exchange, Photochemical Activity of Photosystem II, and Antioxidant Balance in Cyclocarya paliurus to Light Spectra
text: This study investigated the effects of different light spectra (red, blue, white, and a combination of red and blue) on the morphological characteristics, gas exchange parameters, photochemical activity of photosystem II (PSII), and antioxidant balance in Cyclocarya paliurus seedlings. Results revealed that red light significantly enhanced stem elongation and leaf expansion, whereas blue light promoted leaf thickness and chlorophyll content. Gas exchange analysis indicated that the combination of red and blue light optimized photosynthetic rate (Pn), stomatal conductance (gs), and water use efficiency (WUE) compared to monochromatic treatments. Chlorophyll fluorescence measurements demonstrated that blue light and the red-blue combination improved the maximum quantum yield of PSII (Fv/Fm) and photochemical quenching (qP), suggesting enhanced photosynthetic efficiency. Furthermore, plants grown under blue light exhibited lower malondialdehyde (MDA) levels and higher activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD), peroxidase (POD), and catalase (CAT), indicating a more effective antioxidant defense system. Conversely, monochromatic red light induced oxidative stress, as evidenced by elevated MDA accumulation and reduced antioxidant enzyme activities. These findings highlight the importance of light spectrum composition in regulating growth, photosynthesis, and stress resilience in C. paliurus, providing insights for optimizing cultivation practices in controlled environments.

title: Global commitments and China's endeavors to promote health and achieve sustainable development goals
text:
Global Commitments and China's Endeavors to Promote Health and Achieve Sustainable Development Goals

Abstract  
The pursuit of global health and sustainable development has become a cornerstone of international cooperation in the 21st century. Aligned with the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being), nations worldwide have committed to addressing health disparities and fostering resilient health systems. China, as a key global actor, has integrated these commitments into its national agenda through policy innovation, infrastructure investment, and international collaboration. This study examines China’s strategies to promote health equity, enhance healthcare accessibility, and advance SDG 3, while evaluating its contributions to global health governance. By analyzing policy frameworks, health outcomes, and cross-border initiatives, the paper highlights China’s dual role as a domestic innovator and a global health partner.

Keywords  
Sustainable Development Goals, China, Global Health, Healthcare Accessibility, Health Equity, International Collaboration

 1. Introduction  
The adoption of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development in 2015 marked a paradigm shift in global health governance, emphasizing universal health coverage (UHC), pandemic preparedness, and equitable resource allocation. SDG 3, which aims to “ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages,” underscores the interconnectedness of health with economic stability, social inclusion, and environmental resilience. However, achieving this goal requires overcoming systemic challenges such as inadequate infrastructure, workforce shortages, and disparities between urban and rural populations.  

China, home to 18% of the global population, faces unique challenges in balancing rapid urbanization with rural health needs. Despite these hurdles, China has made significant strides in health outcomes, including a 72% reduction in maternal mortality (from 43.2 per 100,000 live births in 2000 to 12.0 in 2022) and a 95% immunization coverage rate for children under five. This paper explores China’s domestic health reforms and its evolving role in global health diplomacy, arguing that its multi-faceted approach offers lessons for low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).

 2. Materials and Methods  
This study employs a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative analysis of health indicators with qualitative assessments of policy documents and international agreements. Data sources include the World Health Organization (WHO), China’s National Health Commission (NHC), and peer-reviewed studies on health equity and SDG progress. Policy analysis focuses on China’s Healthy China 2030 initiative, its rural health revitalization strategy, and contributions to global health mechanisms such as the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) Health Cooperation and the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria.  

Qualitative interviews with 15 policymakers and healthcare professionals in China and Southeast Asia provide insights into the implementation challenges and successes of cross-border health projects. The study also evaluates China’s role in global health emergencies, such as its support for COVID-19 vaccine distribution through COVAX and bilateral donations.

 3. Results and Analysis  
 3.1 Domestic Health Advancements  
China’s Healthy China 2030 plan prioritizes UHC, preventive care, and health technology innovation. By 2023, over 95% of the population was covered by basic medical insurance, with out-of-pocket expenses dropping from 40% of total healthcare spending in 2010 to 27% in 2022. Rural health revitalization efforts have expanded primary care facilities, with 98% of townships now equipped with standardized clinics. Telemedicine adoption in rural areas increased by 400% between 2018 and 2023, improving access to specialists for 60 million residents.  

 3.2 Global Health Contributions  
China’s global health engagement has evolved from bilateral medical aid to multilateral partnerships. Under the BRI Health Cooperation, China has trained 12,000 healthcare workers in 30 countries and constructed 50 hospitals and laboratories. During the COVID-19 pandemic, China provided 2.2 billion vaccine doses to 120 countries, including 1 billion doses as donations. Additionally, China pledged $30 million to the WHO’s ACT-Accelerator in 2021, supporting vaccine equity in LMICs.  

 3.3 Challenges and Gaps  
Despite progress, disparities persist. Rural residents still face a 20% lower life expectancy than urban counterparts, and mental health services remain underdeveloped, with only 10% of patients receiving professional care. Globally, critics argue that China’s health diplomacy sometimes prioritizes geopolitical influence over sustainable capacity-building, as seen in debt-for-health swaps in some BRI nations.

 4. Discussion  
China’s health strategies reflect a blend of authoritarian efficiency and adaptive governance. The centralized healthcare system enables rapid policy rollout, such as the zero-COVID strategy’s initial success in controlling outbreaks. However, decentralized implementation gaps highlight the need for stronger local accountability mechanisms.  

Internationally, China’s “health silk road” model offers an alternative to Western-led aid frameworks by emphasizing infrastructure and technology transfer. Yet, concerns about transparency and long-term debt sustainability underscore the importance of aligning BRI projects with recipient countries’ SDG priorities. Comparatively, China’s vaccine diplomacy outpaced traditional donors in speed but faced scrutiny over data sharing and variant surveillance cooperation.  

To enhance global health equity, China could integrate more community-driven approaches into its BRI projects and strengthen partnerships with multilateral institutions like Gavi and the Global Fund. Domestically, addressing rural-urban disparities requires investing in preventive care and social determinants of health, such as education and environmental protection.

 5. Conclusion  
China’s endeavors to promote health and achieve SDG 3 demonstrate a commitment to balancing national development with global responsibilities. Through policy innovation, infrastructure investment, and international collaboration, China has improved health outcomes domestically and expanded its influence in global health governance. However, persistent inequalities and geopolitical tensions necessitate a more inclusive, transparent approach to health diplomacy.  

Future research should explore the long-term impact of China’s health initiatives on recipient countries’ SDG progress and evaluate the scalability of its rural health models. As the world faces emerging threats like climate change and antimicrobial resistance, China’s role in fostering South-South cooperation and multilateralism will be critical to achieving a healthier, more sustainable future for all.

title: Global greenhouse vegetable production systems are hotspots of soil N2O emissions and nitrogen leaching: A meta-analysis
text: The global demand for fresh vegetables has surged dramatically in recent decades, driven by population growth, urbanization, and shifting dietary preferences toward healthier food options. To meet this escalating demand, greenhouse vegetable production (GVP) systems have emerged as a dominant agricultural practice, particularly in regions with limited arable land or unfavorable climatic conditions. Covering over 5 million hectares worldwide, GVP systems now account for a significant proportion of global vegetable output, offering benefits such as extended growing seasons, enhanced resource use efficiency, and reduced exposure to pests and diseases. However, the intensive management strategies employed in GVP, including high nitrogen (N) fertilizer inputs, frequent irrigation, and elevated soil temperatures, have raised concerns about their environmental sustainability. Notably, these systems have been identified as potential hotspots for soil nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions—a potent greenhouse gas with 298 times the global warming potential of carbon dioxide over a 100-year period—and nitrogen (N) leaching, which contributes to eutrophication and groundwater contamination. Despite the ecological and agricultural significance of GVP systems, a comprehensive quantitative synthesis of their contributions to N₂O emissions and N leaching remains lacking. This meta-analysis addresses this gap by systematically evaluating existing peer-reviewed studies to quantify the magnitude of N₂O emissions and N leaching from GVP systems globally, identify key drivers influencing these processes, and compare their environmental impacts with those of open-field vegetable production. Our findings provide critical insights for optimizing N management in GVP systems to mitigate environmental risks while ensuring food security.

title: Test study of the optimal design for hydraulic performance and treatment performance of free water surface flow constructed wetland
text:
Results and Discussion  

The experimental results revealed significant interactions between design parameters and performance metrics in the free water surface flow (FWS) constructed wetland. Hydraulic retention time (HRT) emerged as the most critical factor influencing both hydraulic and treatment efficiencies. At an HRT of 4 days, the system achieved 82% ± 3% removal of biochemical oxygen demand (BOD₅) and 75% ± 4% nitrogen (TN) removal, compared to 65% ± 5% BOD₅ and 58% ± 6% TN removal at 2 days (Fig. 1a). This aligns with prior studies emphasizing longer HRTs for enhanced pollutant degradation (Smith et al., 2020). However, extending HRT beyond 4 days yielded diminishing returns, with BOD₅ removal plateauing at 84% ± 2%, suggesting microbial saturation or limited oxygen transfer at higher retention times.  

Substrate composition also significantly impacted performance. Systems with a 2:1 sand-gravel mix outperformed single-substrate configurations, achieving 78% ± 3% TN removal versus 62% ± 5% for gravel-only beds (Fig. 1b). The sand-gravel mix enhanced microbial colonization and nitrification, likely due to its balanced porosity and surface area. Conversely, phosphorus (TP) removal was highest (68% ± 4%) in iron-rich laterite substrates, which adsorbed phosphate ions effectively, consistent with findings by Johnson et al. (2018).  

Plant species selection further modulated treatment outcomes. *Typha latifolia* (cattail) systems removed 12% more TN (80% ± 3%) than *Phragmites australis* (reed) systems (68% ± 5%), attributed to cattail’s deeper root system and higher biomass, which promoted denitrification and nutrient uptake (Fig. 2). However, *Phragmites* demonstrated superior BOD₅ removal (85% ± 2% vs. 82% ± 3%), likely due to its faster root exudation rates enhancing microbial activity.  

Hydraulic efficiency, measured via tracer studies, showed that a 1:3 length-to-width ratio minimized short-circuiting, with a dispersion coefficient (D) of 0.12 m²/day, compared to 0.25 m²/day in 1:1 ratio systems. This confirms that elongated designs improve flow uniformity, enhancing pollutant-microbe contact time.  

These findings underscore the importance of optimizing HRT, substrate composition, plant species, and geometry for balanced hydraulic and treatment performance. Future work should explore cost-effective substrate amendments and climate-resilient plant species to enhance scalability.

title: Synthesis and Antibacterial Evaluation of N-phenylacetamide Derivatives Containing 4-arylthiazole Moieties
text:
Synthesis and Antibacterial Evaluation of N-phenylacetamide Derivatives Containing 4-arylthiazole Moieties

Abstract  
This study reports the synthesis and antibacterial evaluation of a series of N-phenylacetamide derivatives incorporating 4-arylthiazole moieties. A total of 12 compounds were designed and synthesized via a two-step protocol involving thiazole ring formation followed by amide coupling. The structures were confirmed using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, mass spectrometry, and infrared (IR) analysis. Antibacterial activity was assessed against Gram-positive (*Staphylococcus aureus* ATCC 25923, *Bacillus subtilis* ATCC 6633) and Gram-negative (*Escherichia coli* ATCC 25922, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* ATCC 27853) bacteria using the broth microdilution method. Compounds 5c and 5f exhibited the highest potency, with minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) ranging from 4 to 16 μg/mL against *S. aureus* and *B. subtilis*. Structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis revealed that electron-withdrawing substituents on the phenyl ring enhanced activity against Gram-positive strains, while bulky groups reduced efficacy. Molecular docking studies suggested binding to the bacterial DNA gyrase enzyme as a plausible mechanism. These findings highlight the potential of 4-arylthiazole-containing N-phenylacetamides as leads for antibacterial drug development.

Keywords: N-phenylacetamide, 4-arylthiazole, antibacterial activity, synthesis, structure-activity relationship.

1. Introduction  
The rise of antibiotic-resistant bacteria poses a critical threat to global health, necessitating the exploration of novel scaffolds with diverse mechanisms of action [1]. Thiazole derivatives are privileged heterocyclic structures widely recognized for their antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral properties [2]. Among these, 4-arylthiazoles have demonstrated significant activity against Gram-positive pathogens, attributed to their ability to disrupt bacterial cell wall synthesis or inhibit essential enzymes like DNA gyrase [3]. Concurrently, N-phenylacetamide moieties have shown promise in medicinal chemistry due to their structural similarity to amide-based antibiotics such as β-lactams [4]. Combining these two pharmacophores—4-arylthiazole and N-phenylacetamide—may yield hybrid molecules with enhanced antibacterial efficacy and reduced resistance development.

Despite the documented biological relevance of thiazoles and acetamides, limited studies have explored their synergistic potential in a single molecular framework [5]. This work aims to synthesize a library of N-phenylacetamide derivatives substituted with 4-arylthiazole moieties and evaluate their antibacterial activity against clinically relevant pathogens. The study also investigates structure-activity relationships (SARs) to identify key structural features influencing potency.

2. Materials and Methods  
2.1. Chemistry  
All reagents and solvents were purchased from commercial suppliers (Sigma-Aldrich, TCI Chemicals) and used without further purification. Melting points were determined using a Stuart SMP30 melting point apparatus. NMR spectra were recorded on a Bruker Avance III 400 MHz spectrometer (DMSO-d₆ as solvent). Mass spectra were obtained via electron ionization (EI) on an Agilent 5975C GC-MS system. IR spectra were recorded on a Shimadzu IRTracer-100 FT-IR spectrometer.

2.1.1. Synthesis of 4-Arylthiazole-2-amine (3a–3d)  
A mixture of aryl ketones (1a–1d, 10 mmol), thiourea (1.52 g, 20 mmol), and iodine (2.54 g, 10 mmol) in ethanol (50 mL) was refluxed for 6 hours. The precipitate was filtered, washed with cold ethanol, and recrystallized from ethanol/water (1:1) to yield intermediates 3a–3d (yield: 65–78%).

2.1.2. Synthesis of N-phenylacetamide Derivatives (5a–5l)  
To a solution of 3a–3d (5 mmol) in dichloromethane (20 mL), triethylamine (0.7 mL, 5 mmol) and phenylacetyl chloride (0.7 mL, 5 mmol) were added dropwise at 0 °C. The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 12 hours, quenched with water, and extracted with dichloromethane. The organic layer was dried over anhydrous Na₂SO₄ and concentrated under reduced pressure. The crude product was purified via column chromatography (hexane/ethyl acetate, 8:2) to afford 5a–5l (yield: 58–72%).

2.2. Antibacterial Activity Assay  
The antibacterial activity of compounds 5a–5l was evaluated using the broth microdilution method following Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines [6]. Test strains included *S. aureus* ATCC 25923, *B. subtilis* ATCC 6633, *E. coli* ATCC 25922, and *P. aeruginosa* ATCC 27853. Stock solutions (1 mg/mL) were prepared in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and diluted in Mueller-Hinton broth to achieve final concentrations ranging from 1 to 256 μg/mL. Ciprofloxacin (1–16 μg/mL) served as the positive control. The MIC was defined as the lowest concentration inhibiting visible bacterial growth after 24 hours of incubation at 37 °C.

2.3. Molecular Docking Studies  
Molecular docking was performed using AutoDock Vina 1.1.2 to investigate binding interactions between compound 5c (the most active derivative) and *E. coli* DNA gyrase (PDB ID: 1AB4) [7]. The protein structure was prepared by removing water molecules and adding polar hydrogens. The ligand was optimized using the MMFF94 force field in Avogadro 1.2.0. Docking simulations were conducted with a grid box size of 20 × 20 × 20 Å centered on the ATP-binding site.

3. Results and Analysis  
3.1. Synthesis and Characterization  
Twelve N-phenylacetamide derivatives (5a–5l) were synthesized with yields ranging from 58% to 72%. The structures were confirmed by NMR, MS, and IR spectroscopy. For example, compound 5c (R¹ = 4-Cl, R² = H) exhibited a molecular ion peak at *m/z* 345.1 (M⁺) in the mass spectrum, consistent with its calculated molecular weight. The IR spectrum showed a strong carbonyl stretch at 1680 cm⁻¹, indicative of the amide group.

3.2. Antibacterial Activity  
The MIC values of 5a–5l against the tested strains are summarized in Table 1. Compounds 5c (R¹ = 4-Cl, R² = H) and 5f (R¹ = 2-NO₂, R² = H) demonstrated the highest potency against Gram-positive bacteria, with MICs of 4–8 μg/mL against *S. aureus* and 8–16 μg/mL against *B. subtilis*. In contrast, most derivatives showed limited activity against Gram-negative strains (MICs > 64 μg/mL), except for 5i (R¹ = 4-F, R² = CH₃), which inhibited *E. coli* at 32 μg/mL. Ciprofloxacin exhibited MICs of 0.5–2 μg/mL across all strains.

Table 1. Antibacterial Activity (MIC, μg/mL) of Compounds 5a–5l  
| Compound | R¹       | R²   | *S. aureus* | *B. subtilis* | *E. coli* | *P. aeruginosa* |
|----------|----------|------|-------------|----------------|-----------|------------------|
| 5a   | H        | H    | 32          | 64             | >256      | >256             |
| 5b   | 4-CH₃    | H    | 16          | 32             | >256      | >256             |
| 5c   | 4-Cl     | H    | 4           | 8              | 128       | 256              |
| 5d   | 4-Br     | H    | 8           | 16             | 256       | >256             |

3.3. Molecular Docking  
Docking results for 5c revealed strong interactions with the ATP-binding pocket of DNA gyrase. The thiazole nitrogen formed a hydrogen bond with Asp73, while the phenyl ring engaged in π-π stacking with Tyr112. The chlorine atom at the 4-position contributed to hydrophobic interactions with Ala79 and Leu83, stabilizing the ligand-protein complex (binding energy: −8.2 kcal/mol).

4. Discussion  
The antibacterial data indicate that electron-withdrawing substituents (e.g., Cl, NO₂) on the phenyl ring of the 4-arylthiazole moiety enhance activity against Gram-positive bacteria. This trend aligns with previous studies suggesting that halogenated thiazoles disrupt bacterial membrane integrity or inhibit efflux pumps [8]. The reduced efficacy against Gram-negative strains may stem from their outer membrane barrier and efflux mechanisms, which limit compound penetration [9].

The SAR analysis highlights the importance of substituent position and size. Ortho-substituted derivatives (5e, 5f) showed comparable or slightly lower potency than their para-substituted counterparts (5c, 5d), possibly due to steric hindrance near the thiazole ring. Methylation of the N-phenylacetamide nitrogen (5i, 5j) improved activity against *E. coli*, suggesting that increased lipophilicity enhances membrane permeability.

Molecular docking supports DNA gyrase as a plausible target, consistent with the activity profile of known gyrase inhibitors like ciprofloxacin [10]. The binding mode of 5c suggests that hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions are critical for inhibitory activity. Future studies will focus on optimizing these interactions through structural modifications.

5. Conclusion  
This study successfully synthesized and evaluated a series of N-phenylacetamide derivatives containing 4-arylthiazole moieties. Compounds 5c and 5f emerged as promising leads against Gram-positive bacteria, with MIC values comparable to early-stage antibiotics. SAR analysis underscored the significance of electron-withdrawing substituents and lipophilicity in modulating activity. Molecular docking provided insights into the potential mechanism of action via DNA gyrase inhibition. These findings warrant further exploration of this hybrid scaffold for antibacterial drug development, including in vivo studies and resistance profiling.

title: Suitable nitrogen application mode and lateral spacing for drip-irrigated winter wheat in North China Plain
text:
Title: Suitable Nitrogen Application Mode and Lateral Spacing for Drip-Irrigated Winter Wheat in North China Plain

Abstract
The North China Plain (NCP) is a critical agricultural region, with winter wheat being a staple crop. Efficient nitrogen (N) management and irrigation practices are essential for enhancing yield while minimizing environmental impacts. This study aimed to determine the optimal nitrogen application mode and drip irrigation lateral spacing for winter wheat in the NCP. A two-year field experiment was conducted with three nitrogen application modes (conventional broadcasting, fertigation at jointing stage, and split fertigation at tillering and jointing stages) and three lateral spacings (30 cm, 45 cm, and 60 cm). Results indicated that split fertigation significantly increased grain yield by 12.5% and nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) by 18.2% compared to conventional broadcasting. A lateral spacing of 45 cm provided the highest yield (6.8 t/ha) and water use efficiency (WUE), balancing water distribution and root zone coverage. These findings suggest that split fertigation combined with 45 cm lateral spacing is optimal for drip-irrigated winter wheat in the NCP, offering a sustainable approach to intensify agriculture while conserving resources.

Keywords: Drip irrigation, nitrogen management, winter wheat, North China Plain, yield, water use efficiency.

Introduction
The North China Plain (NCP) is one of the most important agricultural production regions in China, contributing significantly to the national grain output, particularly winter wheat (*Triticum aestivum* L.). However, the region faces challenges such as water scarcity, declining groundwater levels, and inefficient nutrient use, primarily due to conventional flood irrigation and excessive nitrogen (N) fertilization practices. These practices not only reduce resource use efficiency but also contribute to environmental pollution through nitrate leaching and greenhouse gas emissions.

Drip irrigation, an advanced water-saving technology, has shown promise in improving water and nutrient use efficiencies in various crops by delivering water and nutrients directly to the root zone, reducing evaporation losses, and minimizing runoff. However, the effectiveness of drip irrigation depends on appropriate management practices, including nitrogen application mode and lateral spacing, which influence water distribution uniformity, root system development, and ultimately crop yield and quality.

Nitrogen is a crucial nutrient for winter wheat growth, influencing tillering, spikelet formation, and grain filling. Traditional nitrogen application methods, such as broadcasting before sowing, often lead to N losses through volatilization, denitrification, and leaching, resulting in low nitrogen use efficiency (NUE). Fertigation, the application of fertilizers through irrigation systems, allows for precise timing and placement of nutrients, potentially enhancing NUE and reducing environmental impacts.

Lateral spacing in drip irrigation systems affects the wetted soil volume and the extent of root zone coverage. Optimal spacing ensures uniform water and nutrient distribution, promoting balanced plant growth and minimizing water stress. However, excessively narrow spacing increases installation costs and may lead to competition for water and nutrients among plants, while overly wide spacing can result in inadequate coverage and reduced yield.

Despite the potential benefits of drip irrigation and optimized nitrogen management, limited research has been conducted on the combined effects of nitrogen application mode and lateral spacing on winter wheat performance in the NCP. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the suitable nitrogen application mode and lateral spacing for drip-irrigated winter wheat in the NCP, focusing on yield, NUE, and water use efficiency (WUE).

Materials and Methods
2.1 Site Description
The experiment was conducted over two growing seasons (2020–2021 and 2021–2022) at the Experimental Station of China Agricultural University, located in the NCP (36°N, 116°E). The soil is a typical fluvo-aquic soil with a field capacity of 24.5%, permanent wilting point of 8.2%, and initial soil nitrate-N content of 15.3 mg/kg at a 0–60 cm depth. The climate is temperate monsoon, with an average annual precipitation of 500 mm, primarily occurring from June to September.

2.2 Experimental Design
The experiment was laid out in a split-plot design with three replicates. The main plots consisted of three nitrogen application modes: (1) conventional broadcasting (CB): 225 kg N/ha applied as urea before sowing; (2) fertigation at jointing stage (FJ): 225 kg N/ha applied through drip irrigation at the jointing stage; and (3) split fertigation (SF): 112.5 kg N/ha applied at tillering and 112.5 kg N/ha at jointing stages through drip irrigation. The sub-plots comprised three lateral spacings: 30 cm, 45 cm, and 60 cm. Each sub-plot was 6 m wide and 10 m long.

2.3 Crop Management
Winter wheat (cv. ‘Jimai 22’) was sown at a seed rate of 187.5 kg/ha in mid-October each year and harvested in early June the following year. Phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) fertilizers were applied as basal doses at rates of 120 kg P₂O₅/ha and 90 kg K₂O/ha, respectively, for all treatments. Drip irrigation was scheduled based on soil moisture content, maintaining it above 60% of field capacity. Pests, diseases, and weeds were controlled using recommended agrochemicals.

2.4 Data Collection and Analysis
Grain yield was determined by harvesting three 1 m² areas from each sub-plot at maturity and adjusting to a 14% moisture content. Nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) was calculated as the ratio of grain N uptake to total N applied. Water use efficiency (WUE) was computed as the ratio of grain yield to seasonal evapotranspiration (ET), estimated using the water balance method. Soil water content was monitored using Time Domain Reflectometry (TDR) probes at 20 cm intervals down to 60 cm depth. Data were analyzed using ANOVA (SAS Institute, Cary, NC), and means were separated using LSD at p ≤ 0.05.

Results
3.1 Grain Yield
Nitrogen application mode significantly affected grain yield (p < 0.01). Split fertigation (SF) resulted in the highest yield (6.7 t/ha in 2020–2021 and 6.9 t/ha in 2021–2022), followed by FJ (6.2 and 6.4 t/ha, respectively), and CB (5.9 and 6.1 t/ha, respectively). Lateral spacing also had a significant effect (p < 0.05), with 45 cm spacing yielding the highest (6.8 t/ha averaged over two years), followed by 60 cm (6.5 t/ha) and 30 cm (6.3 t/ha). The interaction between nitrogen mode and spacing was not significant (p > 0.05).

3.2 Nitrogen Use Efficiency (NUE)
SF exhibited the highest NUE (48.5%), significantly greater than FJ (42.3%) and CB (35.1%) (p < 0.01). Lateral spacing did not significantly influence NUE (p > 0.05), averaging 42.7%, 43.1%, and 42.9% for 30 cm, 45 cm, and 60 cm spacings, respectively.

3.3 Water Use Efficiency (WUE)
WUE was significantly affected by both nitrogen mode and lateral spacing (p < 0.01). SF combined with 45 cm spacing achieved the highest WUE (1.98 kg/m³), while CB with 30 cm spacing had the lowest (1.65 kg/m³). Fertigation modes generally improved WUE compared to CB, attributed to more efficient water and N utilization.

Discussion
The superior performance of split fertigation over conventional broadcasting and single fertigation can be attributed to its ability to synchronize N supply with crop demand, reducing N losses and enhancing uptake efficiency. This aligns with previous studies showing that split N applications improve NUE in wheat by minimizing leaching and denitrification losses during periods of low N demand.

The optimal lateral spacing of 45 cm likely balances the need for adequate root zone coverage and uniform water distribution. Narrower spacings (30 cm) may lead to excessive overlap of wetted zones, causing waterlogging and competition for resources, while wider spacings (60 cm) may result in insufficient soil moisture and nutrient availability, particularly during critical growth stages.

The lack of significant interaction between nitrogen mode and spacing suggests that the benefits of split fertigation are consistent across different lateral configurations, providing flexibility in system design. However, the higher WUE observed with 45 cm spacing indicates that this spacing may be more suitable for the NCP’s soil and climatic conditions, where water conservation is paramount.

Conclusion
This study demonstrates that split fertigation combined with a 45 cm lateral spacing is the most suitable approach for drip-irrigated winter wheat in the North China Plain, resulting in higher grain yield, NUE, and WUE compared to conventional practices. These findings support the adoption of precision nitrogen and irrigation management strategies to enhance agricultural sustainability in water-limited regions. Future research should focus on long-term impacts and economic feasibility to promote widespread implementation among farmers.

title: Exploring polyamines: Functions in embryo/fetal development
text:
Polyamines (putrescine, spermidine, and spermine) are ubiquitous polycationic compounds essential for cellular proliferation, differentiation, and survival. Their roles in embryo/fetal development have garnered significant attention due to their dynamic regulation during critical periods of organogenesis and tissue maturation. This review synthesizes current knowledge on polyamine functions in prenatal development, emphasizing their involvement in epigenetic modulation, cell signaling, and antioxidant defense. Polyamines interact with nucleic acids to stabilize chromatin structure and regulate gene expression, influencing pluripotency and lineage commitment in embryonic stem cells. They also modulate key developmental pathways, including Wnt/β-catenin and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), to coordinate cell proliferation and tissue patterning. Furthermore, polyamines mitigate oxidative stress by scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS) and preserving mitochondrial function, thereby protecting developing embryos from environmental insults. Disruptions in polyamine homeostasis, caused by genetic deficiencies or maternal dietary restrictions, are linked to developmental abnormalities such as neural tube defects and intrauterine growth restriction. Therapeutic interventions targeting polyamine metabolism, including supplementation with precursors or inhibitors, demonstrate potential in preclinical models to ameliorate such defects. However, challenges remain in optimizing delivery systems and minimizing off-target effects. Future research should prioritize elucidating tissue-specific mechanisms and long-term outcomes of polyamine modulation during gestation. Understanding these processes may advance strategies for preventing congenital disorders and improving perinatal health.

title: Bacterial seed endophyte shapes disease resistance in rice
text:
Bacterial Seed Endophyte Shapes Disease Resistance in Rice

Abstract  
Rice (*Oryza sativa*) is a staple crop critical for global food security, yet its production is threatened by pathogens such as *Magnaporthe oryzae* (rice blast) and *Xanthomonas oryzae* pv. *oryzae* (bacterial leaf blight). Seed-borne endophytes, symbiotic bacteria residing within plant tissues, have emerged as potential biocontrol agents due to their role in enhancing host immunity and suppressing pathogens. This study investigates the impact of a novel bacterial seed endophyte, *Bacillus velezensis* strain RZB2, on disease resistance in rice. Through greenhouse and field trials, we demonstrate that seed treatment with RZB2 significantly reduces disease severity caused by *M. oryzae* and *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae*. Transcriptomic analysis reveals upregulation of pathogenesis-related (PR) genes and salicylic acid (SA) signaling pathways in RZB2-treated plants, suggesting priming of systemic acquired resistance (SAR). Additionally, RZB2 produces antifungal lipopeptides (e.g., surfactin and iturin) and siderophores, which directly inhibit pathogen growth. Our findings highlight the dual mechanism of RZB2—direct antagonism and induced systemic resistance—as a promising strategy for sustainable rice disease management.

Keywords: Rice, Seed endophyte, *Bacillus velezensis*, Disease resistance, Systemic acquired resistance, Biocontrol.

---

 1. Introduction  
Rice is the primary food source for over half the global population, but its yield is severely constrained by diseases such as rice blast and bacterial leaf blight, which cause annual losses exceeding 30% in epidemic years [1]. Conventional disease control relies on chemical fungicides and antibiotics, which pose risks to human health and environmental sustainability [2]. The exploration of microbial biocontrol agents, particularly seed-borne endophytes, offers an eco-friendly alternative by leveraging plant-microbe interactions to enhance disease resistance [3].

Seed endophytes are vertically transmitted bacteria that colonize internal plant tissues without causing harm. They contribute to host fitness by producing antimicrobial compounds, modulating plant immunity, and competing with pathogens for nutrients [4]. Among these, *Bacillus* species are widely studied for their ability to produce bioactive secondary metabolites and induce systemic resistance (ISR) [5]. For instance, *Bacillus velezensis* strains have been shown to suppress soil-borne pathogens in tomato and wheat via lipopeptide synthesis and activation of jasmonic acid (JA)-dependent defenses [6,7]. However, their role in seed-mediated disease resistance in rice remains underexplored.

This study identifies *Bacillus velezensis* strain RZB2, isolated from healthy rice seeds, as a potent inducer of disease resistance against *M. oryzae* and *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae*. We hypothesize that RZB2 employs a two-pronged strategy: (1) direct inhibition of pathogens through antimicrobial compounds and (2) priming of plant immunity via salicylic acid (SA)-dependent signaling. To test this, we evaluated disease incidence under greenhouse and field conditions, analyzed RZB2’s bioactive metabolites, and profiled transcriptional changes in host defense pathways.

---

 2. Materials and Methods  

 2.1 Bacterial Strain and Culture Conditions  
*Bacillus velezensis* RZB2 was isolated from surface-sterilized rice seeds (*Oryza sativa* cv. Nipponbare) using nutrient agar (NA) medium. The strain was identified via 16S rRNA sequencing (GenBank accession no. ON123456) and stored in glycerol at −80°C. For experiments, RZB2 was cultured in Luria-Bertani (LB) broth at 30°C with shaking (180 rpm) for 48 h.

 2.2 Seed Treatment and Plant Growth Conditions  
Rice seeds were surface-sterilized (70% ethanol for 2 min, 2% NaClO for 5 min) and soaked in RZB2 suspension (10⁸ CFU/mL) or sterile water (control) for 24 h. Seedlings were grown in a greenhouse (28°C, 16 h light/8 h dark) in pots containing autoclaved soil. For field trials, seeds were sown in plots (5 m × 5 m) at the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI), Philippines, during the wet season (June–October 2023).

 2.3 Disease Assays  
- Rice Blast: Three-week-old seedlings were sprayed with a conidial suspension of *M. oryzae* strain Guy11 (10⁵ spores/mL). Disease severity was scored 7 days post-inoculation (dpi) using a 0–5 scale (0 = no lesions; 5 = >50% leaf area affected) [8].
- Bacterial Leaf Blight: Four-week-old plants were infiltrated with *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* strain PXO99 (10⁸ CFU/mL). Lesion length was measured at 14 dpi.

 2.4 Antimicrobial Compound Analysis  
RZB2 was grown in Landy medium for 72 h, and culture supernatants were extracted with ethyl acetate. Antifungal activity was tested against *M. oryzae* using a disk diffusion assay (10 µL supernatant per disk). Lipopeptides (surfactin, iturin, fengycin) were quantified via HPLC-MS, and siderophores were detected using chrome azurol S (CAS) agar [9].

 2.5 Transcriptomic Analysis  
Leaf samples from RZB2-treated and control plants were collected at 0, 24, and 48 h post-inoculation (hpi) with *M. oryzae*. RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent, and libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using DESeq2 (|log₂FC| ≥ 1, FDR < 0.05). Pathway enrichment was performed with MapMan [10].

 2.6 Statistical Analysis  
Data were analyzed using R v4.1.2. Disease scores and lesion lengths were compared using ANOVA with Tukey’s HSD test (p < 0.05). Transcriptomic data were visualized with ggplot2.

---

 3. Results and Analysis  

 3.1 RZB2 Reduces Disease Severity in Rice  
In greenhouse trials, RZB2-treated plants exhibited a 62% reduction in rice blast severity (mean score: 1.2 ± 0.3) compared to controls (3.2 ± 0.5; p < 0.001; Fig. 1A). Similarly, bacterial leaf blight lesion length decreased by 54% (12.3 ± 2.1 mm vs. 26.7 ± 3.4 mm; p < 0.001; Fig. 1B). Field trials confirmed these results, with RZB2 reducing blast incidence by 48% and bacterial blight by 39% (Fig. 1C–D).

 3.2 RZB2 Produces Antimicrobial Metabolites  
HPLC-MS detected surfactin (12.3 ± 1.2 µg/mL), iturin (8.7 ± 0.9 µg/mL), and fengycin (5.4 ± 0.6 µg/mL) in RZB2 supernatants. CAS assays revealed siderophore production (orange halos around colonies). Disk diffusion assays showed that RZB2 supernatants inhibited *M. oryzae* growth by 78% relative to LB controls (Fig. 2A–B).

 3.3 RZB2 Primes SA-Dependent Defense Pathways  
Transcriptomic analysis identified 1,245 DEGs between RZB2-treated and control plants at 24 hpi with *M. oryzae*. KEGG enrichment highlighted upregulation of SA biosynthesis (ICS1, PBS3) and signaling (PR1, PR5, NPR1) genes (Fig. 3A). Conversely, JA/ET pathway genes (LOX2, PDF1.2) were downregulated, suggesting SA dominance in RZB2-induced resistance (Fig. 3B).

 3.4 RZB2 Colonization Is Asymptomatic and Persistent  
qPCR analysis confirmed RZB2 colonization in rice roots (10⁵ CFU/g tissue) and shoots (10³ CFU/g tissue) at 30 days post-sowing. No visible symptoms were observed, indicating endophytic lifestyle compatibility.

---

 4. Discussion  
This study demonstrates that *Bacillus velezensis* RZB2 enhances rice disease resistance through dual mechanisms: direct pathogen suppression and induction of SA-mediated SAR. The production of antifungal lipopeptides (surfactin, iturin) and siderophores aligns with previous reports on *Bacillus* spp. [11], explaining RZB2’s efficacy against both fungal and bacterial pathogens. Notably, RZB2’s ability to colonize seeds and persist in plants suggests its suitability for long-term disease protection.

Transcriptomic data reveal that RZB2 primes SA signaling, a key pathway for defense against biotrophic pathogens like *M. oryzae* [12]. The downregulation of JA/ET-responsive genes further supports a trade-off between SA and JA defenses, a common phenomenon in plant immunity [13]. This priming effect may reduce the metabolic cost of defense activation, enhancing crop resilience under field conditions.

Field trials validate the practicality of RZB2 as a biocontrol agent, showing consistent disease reduction despite environmental variability. However, the efficacy of RZB2 under diverse agroclimatic conditions remains to be tested. Additionally, combining RZB2 with reduced fungicide doses could optimize sustainability, though potential synergy or antagonism requires further study.

---

 5. Conclusion  
*Bacillus velezensis* RZB2 represents a promising seed treatment for enhancing rice disease resistance. Its dual mode of action—direct pathogen inhibition and SA-dependent immune priming—provides robust protection against major rice pathogens. Future research should focus on optimizing application methods, exploring synergies with other biocontrol agents, and assessing long-term ecological impacts. By harnessing seed endophytes like RZB2, we can advance sustainable agriculture and reduce reliance on chemical inputs.

---
